💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we gave Claude the ability to fine-tune language models using a upcoming tool called Hugging Face Skills.
  • Claude Code can use "skills"—packaged instructions, scripts, and domain knowledge—to accomplish specialized tasks.
  • The model trains on Hugging Face GPUs while you do other things.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we gave Claude the ability to fine-tune language models using a upcoming tool called Hugging Face Skills. Not just write training scripts, but to actually submit jobs to cloud GPUs, monitor progress, and push finished models to the Hugging Face Hub. This tutorial demonstrates you how it works and how to use it yourself.

Claude Code can use "skills"—packaged instructions, scripts, and domain knowledge—to accomplish specialized tasks. The hf-llm-trainer skill teaches Claude everything it needs to know about training: which GPU to pick for your model size, how to configure Hub authentication, when to use LoRA versus full fine-tuning, and how to handle the dozens of other decisions that go into a successful training run.

With this skill, you can tell Claude things like:.

The model trains on Hugging Face GPUs while you do other things. When it's done, your fine-tuned model appears on the Hub, ready to use.

It has been revealed that this isn't a toy demo. The skill supports the same training methods used in production: supervised fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. You can train models from 0.5B to 70B parameters, convert them to GGUF for local deployment, and run multi-stage pipelines that combine different techniques.

It has been revealed that hugging Face skills are compatible with Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI. With integrations on the way for Cursor, Windsurf, and Continue.

This repo includes gemini-extension.json to integrate with the Gemini CLI.

You have to authenticate to your Hugging Face account with a write-access token so that the job can create a model repo.

Configure Hugging Face MCP Server to use your write token by sending it in either the HF_TOKEN or Authorization: Bearer HTTP Headers.

For Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http hf-skills https://huggingface.co/mcp?bouquet=skills --header "Authorization: Bearer $HF_TOKEN".

Let's walk through a complete example. We'll fine-tune a small model to see the full workflow, then explore more advanced capabilities.

Start with a simple and clear instruction to fine tune a specific model.

In a recent development, the coding agent analyzes your request and prepares a training configuration. For a 0.6B model on a demo dataset, it selects t4-small—enough GPU for this model size and the cheapest option available.

In a recent development, the open-r1/codeforces-cots dataset is a dataset of codeforces problems and solutions. It is a good dataset for instruction tuning a model to solve hard coding problems.

In a recent development, this works for vision language models too! You can simply run "Fine-tune Qwen/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct on llava-instruct-mix".

Before your coding agent submits anything, you'll see the configuration:.

According to recent reports, this is your chance to adjust anything. Change the output repo name, pick different hardware, or ask Claude to modify training parameters. Once you approve, the agent submits the job.

For example, you can ask the agent to try a test run:.

After submission, you get job details:.

The skill includes Trackio integration, so you can watch training loss decrease in real-time. Jobs run asynchronously so you can close your terminal and come back later. When you want an enhancement:.

Then the agent fetches the logs and summarizes progress.

When training completes, your model is on the Hub:.

That's the full loop. You described what you wanted in plain English, and the agent handled GPU selection, script generation, job submission, authentication, and persistence. The whole thing cost about thirty cents.

According to recent reports, the skill supports three training approaches. Understanding when to use each one helps you get better results.

Sources indicate that SFT is where most projects start. You provide demonstration data—examples of inputs and desired outputs—and training adjusts the model to match those patterns.

Recent findings suggest that use SFT when you have high-quality examples of the behavior you want. Customer support conversations, code generation pairs, domain-specific Q&A—anything where you can show the model what good looks like.

The agent validates the dataset, selects hardware (a10g-large with LoRA for a 7B model), and configures training with checkpoints and monitoring.

In a recent development, for models larger than 3B parameters, the agent automatically uses LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) to reduce memory requirements. This makes training 7B or 13B models feasible on single GPUs while preserving most of the quality of full fine-tuning.

DPO trains on preference pairs—responses where one is "chosen" and another is "rejected." This aligns model outputs with human preferences, typically after an initial SFT stage.

Use DPO when you have preference annotations from human labelers or automated comparisons. DPO optimizes directly for the preferred response without needing a separate reward model.

Recent findings suggest that DPO is sensitive to dataset format. It requires columns named exactly chosen and rejected, or a prompt column with the input. The agent validates this first and shows you how to map columns if your dataset uses different names.

You can run DPO using Skills on vision language models too! Try it out with openbmb/RLAIF-V-Dataset. Claude will apply minor modifications but will succeed in training.

GRPO is a reinforcement learning task that is proven to be effective on verifiable tasks like solving math problems, writing code, or any task with a programmatic success criterion.

It has been revealed that the model generates responses, receives rewards based on correctness, and learns from the outcomes. This is more complex than SFT or DPO, but the configuration is similar.

The agent selects hardware based on your model size, but understanding the tradeoffs helps you make better decisions.

For tiny models under 1B parameters, t4-small works well. These models train promptly—expect $1-2 for a full run. This is perfect for educational or experimental runs.

It has been revealed that for small models (1-3B), step up to t4-medium or a10g-small. Training takes a few hours and costs $5-15.

Sources indicate that for medium models (3-7B), you need a10g-large or a100-large with LoRA. Full fine-tuning doesn't fit, but LoRA makes these very trainable. Budget $15-40 for production.

For large models (7B+), this HF skills job is not suitable.

When testing a workflow, start small:.

The coding agent configures minimal training—enough to verify your pipeline works without real cost.

Industry observers note that always run a demo before committing to a multi-hour production job. A $0.50 demo that catches a format error saves a $30 failed run.

Dataset format is the most common source of training failures. The agent can validate datasets before you spend GPU time.

The agent runs a quick inspection on CPU (fractions of a penny) and reports:.

If your dataset needs transformation, the agent can show you how:.

The agent provides mapping code and can incorporate it directly into your training script.

Industry observers note that real-time monitoring helps you catch problems early. The skill configures Trackio by default—after submitting a job, you can watch metrics at:.

Industry observers note that this shows training loss, learning rate, and validation metrics. A healthy run shows steadily decreasing loss.

Ask the agent about status anytime:.

Industry observers note that if something goes wrong, the agent helps diagnose. Out of memory? the agent suggests reducing batch size or upgrading hardware. Dataset error? The agent identifies the mismatch. Timeout? The agent recommends longer duration or faster training settings.

After training, you might want to run your model locally. The GGUF format works with llama.cpp and dependent tools like LM Studio, Ollama, etc.

The agent submits a conversion job that merges LoRA adapters, converts to GGUF, applies quantization, and pushes to Hub.

We've shown that coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI can handle the full lifecycle of model fine-tuning: validating data, selecting hardware, generating scripts, submitting jobs, monitoring progress, and converting outputs. This turns what used to be a specialized skill into something you can do through conversation.

In a recent development, the skill is open source. You can extend it, customize it for your workflows, or use it as a starting point for other training scenarios.

#80632. Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks: Why Learnable Functions on Edges Beat Fixed Activations

Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks: Why Learnable Functions on Edges Beat Fixed Activations

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every multilayer perceptron is built on the same deal: the edges carry numbers and the nodes carry the nonlinearity.
  • In a recent development, the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, proved in 1957, states that any continuous multivariate function on a bounded domain can be written as a finite composition of continuous univariate functions and addition.
  • It claims a function of n variables never needs a genuinely multivariate nonlinearity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every multilayer perceptron is built on the same deal: the edges carry numbers and the nodes carry the nonlinearity. A weight multiplies a signal, a fixed activation such as ReLU or GELU bends it, and the network learns by adjusting the numbers. It works, but the deal is arbitrary. The Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem says there is another way to build a function, one where the edges themselves are learnable functions and the nodes only add. Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, or KANs, take that theorem literally, and the result is a model that is more interpretable, more parameter-efficient on structured problems, and surprisingly good at rediscovering symbolic laws from data.

In a recent development, the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, proved in 1957, states that any continuous multivariate function on a bounded domain can be written as a finite composition of continuous univariate functions and addition. In its two-layer form:.

That is a striking claim. It claims a function of n variables never needs a genuinely multivariate nonlinearity. It only needs univariate functions, applied to single inputs, combined by addition. The outer functions Φq\Phi_qΦq​ and the inner functions ϕq,p\phi_{q,p}ϕq,p​ depend on f, and the theorem says nothing about how smooth they are. In the worst case they can be fractal and pathological, which is why the theorem sat on the shelf for decades as a curiosity rather than a blueprint.

The KAN idea is to turn the theorem into a trainable architecture by restricting those univariate functions to a smooth, parameterised family: B-splines. If the true function is reasonably well behaved, a spline can approximate each univariate piece closely, and the network can learn the decomposition from data. The theorem supplies the structure; the splines supply the learnability.

An MLP layer is a linear map followed by a fixed nonlinearity applied at each node. A KAN layer inverts that arrangement. Every edge carries a learnable univariate function, and every node simply sums its incoming signals:.

Sources indicate that there is no activation function at the node at all. The nonlinearity lives entirely on the edges, inside the ϕl,j,i\phi_{l,j,i}ϕl,j,i​ .

Each edge function is parameterised as a B-spline plus a smooth basis function:.

Here b(x)=x/(1+e−x)b(x) = x / (1 + e^{-x})b(x)=x/(1+e−x) is the SiLU basis, BiB_iBi​ are B-spline basis functions of order k on a grid of size G, and the coefficients cic_ici​ are the learnable parameters. The grid controls resolution: a coarse grid gives a smooth, low-capacity function, while a fine grid can capture sharp features. One practical advantage is grid extension. A KAN trained on a coarse grid can be refined to a finer grid by fitting the finer spline to the learned function, without retraining from scratch. That is the analogue of increasing resolution in a numerical method, and it gives a principled way to add capacity during training.

Stacking layers composes these univariate functions, so a deep KAN can represent functions whose structure is compositional: a sum of functions of sums of functions, and so on. The width of a layer sets how many univariate pieces are available at that stage, just as width in an MLP sets how many features are available.

The first payoff is interpretability. In an MLP, the learned object is a weight matrix, and understanding what a single weight means requires tracing it through the rest of the network. In a KAN, the learned object on each edge is a one-dimensional function, and a one-dimensional function can be plotted. You can look at an edge and see that it learned something close to a sine wave, a logarithm, or a saturating curve. After training, edges whose functions are near zero can be pruned, and the remaining functions can be fitted with symbolic expressions, turning the trained network into a readable formula. That is why KANs have attracted attention in scientific machine learning: when the data come from a physical law, the network has a chance of rediscovering the law rather than merely approximating it.

Recent findings suggest that the second payoff is parameter efficiency on structured problems. A function with a compositional structure, such as f(x,y)=sin⁡(xy)f(x, y) = \sin(x y)f(x,y)=sin(xy) or a polynomial in a few variables, can require a large MLP to approximate to high accuracy, because the MLP must build the structure out of generic piecewise-linear pieces. A KAN can represent the same structure directly, with far fewer parameters. In the original KAN paper, small KANs matched or beat larger MLPs on symbolic regression tasks and on fitting special functions, often by orders of magnitude in parameter count.

It has been revealed that the third payoff is a cleaner inductive bias for low-dimensional problems. Many scientific problems have few inputs and a smooth target with identifiable structure. An MLP treats such a problem as a generic high-dimensional approximation task. A KAN treats it as a composition of univariate pieces, which is a much stronger and often correct prior.

The cleanest demonstration is symbolic regression. Suppose the data come from a function with multiplicative structure, and you want the model to recover it rather than just interpolate it. Using the pykan library, the workflow is short:.

Three things about this workflow are worth noting. First, model.plot() is not a debugging aid; it is the main interpretability tool, because each edge function is a plot. Second, pruning is meaningful in a way weight pruning in an MLP is not: removing an edge removes a whole univariate function, and the surviving graph is a readable decomposition of the target. Third, symbolic_formula() closes the loop from data to equation, which is the point of the exercise. If the learned functions are close to sine, exponential, or polynomial pieces, the symbolic fit recovers them, and you can check the recovered formula against held-out data.

In a recent development, the same pattern applies to real scientific data. Given measurements of a physical system, a KAN can be trained, pruned, and converted to a candidate formula, which a domain expert can then inspect, test, and refine. That is a different workflow from deploying a black-box predictor, and for science it is often the more valuable one.

KANs are not a replacement for MLPs, and the honest limitations matter more than the headline results.

Training is slower. Evaluating a spline on every edge costs more than a matrix multiply followed by a pointwise activation, and the backward pass through the spline coefficients is heavier still. For large models, that cost dominates, and the parameter efficiency on small problems does not translate into a compute advantage at scale.

Sources indicate that scaling behaviour is unsettled. The original paper reported favourable neural scaling laws for KANs on some tasks, but follow-up work has shown MLPs catching up or overtaking KANs as model and data scale grow, particularly on high-dimensional tasks such as vision and language where the target function has little low-dimensional compositional structure to exploit. No KAN has yet matched a transformer on a large language or vision benchmark, and there is no evidence it should.

It has been revealed that optimisation is trickier. Spline coefficients interact with each other in ways that weights in an MLP do not, and the loss landscape can be harder to navigate. Grid extension helps, but choosing the grid size, spline order, and regularisation strength adds hyperparameters that an MLP does not have. Too fine a grid overfits; too coarse a grid underfits; and the right choice depends on the smoothness of the unknown target.

In a recent development, finally, interpretability has a limit. A KAN is interpretable when the true function is compositional and the learned decomposition is sparse. On a genuinely high-dimensional problem with no such structure, the learned edge functions are arbitrary wiggles, and plotting them tells you nothing. Interpretability is a property of the problem as much as of the model.

Sources indicate that use a KAN when the problem is low-dimensional, the target is plausibly a composition of simple univariate functions, and you care about the formula as much as the prediction. Scientific modelling, symbolic regression, and small tabular problems with smooth structure are the natural home. Avoid KANs when the inputs are high-dimensional raw signals, when training speed at scale matters, or when a transformer or a large MLP is already known to work well. In those settings, the MLP's simplicity and speed win.

A practical checklist before training: start with a small width and a coarse grid, and refine the grid only if the fit is underfitting; use the L1-style regularisation on edge magnitudes that the library provides, so pruning has something to work with; plot the edge functions early, not just at the end, because a healthy KAN demonstrates smooth, recognisable curves while a struggling one shows noise; and always validate the symbolic formula on held-out data before believing it, since a spline can fit training noise with a plausible-looking curve.

MLPs put the learning in the weights and the nonlinearity in fixed activations. KANs put the learning in the functions themselves, with one learnable univariate function per edge and nothing but addition at the nodes. The Kolmogorov-Arnold theorem guarantees that such a decomposition exists; B-splines make it trainable. The result is not a universal replacement for the MLP, but a sharper tool for a specific job: low-dimensional, structured problems where the learned function should be inspected, pruned, and ideally read back as a formula. When the problem fits that description, a KAN can do with a handful of parameters what an MLP needs thousands for, and it can show its working.

DeepMath: A lightweight math reasoning Agent with smolagents

📅 04 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (932 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • DeepMath is an aligned math reasoning agent built on Qwen3-4B Thinking and fine-tuned with GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization).
  • We evaluate DeepMath on four math datasets: MATH500, AIME, HMMT, and HLE, and show that:.
  • 🤖 The math agent alone reduces output lengths by up to 66%, while often improving accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DeepMath is an aligned math reasoning agent built on Qwen3-4B Thinking and fine-tuned with GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). Instead of verbose text, the model emits tiny Python snippets for intermediate steps, runs them in a secure sandbox, and folds the results back into its reasoning, reducing errors and output length. The agent is implemented using the smolagents library.

We evaluate DeepMath on four math datasets: MATH500, AIME, HMMT, and HLE, and show that:.

🤖 The math agent alone reduces output lengths by up to 66%, while often improving accuracy.

⚡ GRPO training improves the agent performance even further, in almost all benchmarks.

👉 Code and evaluation scripts: https://github.com/IntelLabs/DeepMath 👉 Model: https://huggingface.co/Intel/deepmath-v1.

Recent findings suggest that large language models (LLMs) have advanced reasoning capabilities, but mathematical problem-solving remains challenging; chain-of-thought traces can be lengthy and prone to arithmetic mistakes. Recent works[^1][^2] demonstrate that small models can reach strong performance, and other studies[^3] investigate tool use to improve reliability. What those papers generally do not emphasize is reducing trace verbosity or explicitly training models to prefer short, computation-oriented traces executed in a constrained, auditable environment.

Offload deterministic computation to a safe executor.

Train models to prefer concise, computation-oriented traces over verbose text.

DeepMath tackles this by combining a small Python executor with a fine-tuned LLM, enabling concise, computation-driven reasoning. The model learns to generate short Python snippets, which are executed in a sandbox and reintegrated into the context. GRPO fine-tuning encourages this behavior by rewarding correctness and encouraging shorter outputs.

Figure 1: The vLLM client and server were modified to use the DeepMath agent in generating the candidates, while using the vLLM backend.

Agent Interface: During inference, the model can output normal tokens or special agent calls containing Python snippets.

Execution: Snippets run in a sandboxed environment with strict safety constraints (no file I/O, no network, timeouts).

Concision: Replace multi-line textual calculations with short, focused snippets.

Determinism & Safety: Enforce strict execution limits.

Interpretability: Snippets are readable and auditable.

Figure 2: Output example where python code is generated, evaluated and the answer is inserted into the trace and used for context.

We fine-tune the model using GRPO, a reward-based optimization that balances:.

Accuracy Reward: +1 for correct answers.

Using code snippets: +1 for generating code snippets, weighted 10:1 vs. the accuracy reward.

Length reduction: shorter lengths are encouraged by limiting the GRPO completion candidates to 5k tokens.

It has been revealed that temperature Scheduling: We implemented linear temperature scheduling (T=1.2 → T=0.7) to balance exploration and stability during training. This approach aims to enhance experimentation during the initial training phases, subsequently reducing the temperature as we refine our proficiency in the skill.

In-context Learning: we include 4 solved examples where the trace contains agent calls and executor outputs, so the model learns the syntax and the call/response pattern.

Sources indicate that dataset: we used the Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) subset of the OpenMathReasoning dataset. Note that GRPO only uses the problem, not the solution in the data. This dataset was chosen to ensure the problems benefit from the external tool.

Recent findings suggest that we benchmarked DeepMath against baselines on four datasets. Metrics include:.

majority@16: robustness across samples, as used in previous math reasoning works, see references.

According to recent reports, we compare a baseline configuration (Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, no agenting) with our DeepMath model. As ablation, we evaluate the agentic framework we developed running with the untrained Qwen3 model, denoted by +Agent. Additionally, we examine whether the GRPO training (for agentic use) improves non-agentic inference, denoted by +GRPO. Thus the two ablations are independent, not additive.

We observe the agentic inference reduces output lengths, with mixed accuracy results. The DeepMath model is both GRPO-trained and run in agentic mode, and shows the highest accuracy with shortened traces. We conclude both GRPO training and agentic inference are needed for best results.

Key Insight: DeepMath reduces output length by up to 66% while improving accuracy on challenging datasets.

Accuracy: Offloading computation reduces arithmetic errors.

Efficiency: Shorter outputs mean faster inference and easier interpretability.

Safety: Sandbox execution mitigates risks of running arbitrary code.

DeepMath demonstrates a practical and lightweight way to combine a small executor with an LLM and to train the model to prefer short, computation-driven traces. Offloading deterministic computation reduces arithmetic and numerical errors and shortens traces, and GRPO fine-tuning further encourages concise, correct answers. The result is a more accurate and more interpretable math-solving agent without requiring a massive model or heavyweight external tools.

Check out the GitHub repo and share your feedback! Contributions welcome. 🚀.

If you use DeepMath in your research, please cite:.

Scope: we focused on a small model and on mathematical reasoning.

Generalization: evaluated on contest-style math; results may not transfer to open-ended mathematical creativity or formal proofs.

Executing generated code is inherently risky. DeepMath uses strict sandboxing and resource limits, but any deployment should carefully manage attack surfaces and enforce rate limits.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • So we priced the same setup on 11 providers at two sizes:.
  • The rules: one database, always on (730 hours), single node with no standby, in London where offered (Railway in Amsterdam, Render in Frankfurt, Heroku in its EU region).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I wanted a plain answer to a plain question: what does it cost to keep one Postgres database running all month on a managed service? Not the "from" price, but the bill once storage and any plan fee you must pay first are added.

So we priced the same setup on 11 providers at two sizes:.

The rules: one database, always on (730 hours), single node with no standby, in London where offered (Railway in Amsterdam, Render in Frankfurt, Heroku in its EU region). Storage and any compulsory initiative fee are included. Prices are in US dollars, before VAT, and were checked in November 2026. They change, so check the vendor's page before you commit.

Sources indicate that heroku is cheapest on paper, but it doesn't publish Essential-1's memory, so it may not match 1 GB. The cheapest with a stated 1 GB are DigitalOcean at $15.15 and AWS RDS at $15.80.

Sources indicate that neon's figure keeps the compute on all month. A Neon database that scales to zero when idle costs less: Neon's own "typical" Launch figure is $15 a month.

Railway's figure is an estimate. It bills the RAM and CPU a service actually uses, and we assumed the database holds all 16 GB and averages 10% of its CPU; each extra 10% adds $8. Heroku's Standard-3 ($400) has only 2 vCPU and 15.25 GB, so Standard-4 is its first strategy that fits.

Almost everyone bills storage separately, per GB a month: Neon $0.35, Render $0.30, Google Cloud SQL $0.204 in London, Railway $0.15, AWS RDS $0.133, and Supabase $0.125 after the 8 GB it includes.

At 200 GB that's a real line on the bill: $70.00 at Neon, $60 at Render, $40.80 at Google Cloud SQL, $30 at Railway and $26.60 at AWS RDS.

Minimums matter at the small end. AWS's gp3 storage starts at 20 GiB, so a 10 GB database pays for 20. Azure's Burstable servers can't go below a 32 GiB disk. Aiven's cheaper looks are fixed at 8 GB of storage, so its cheapest plan that holds 10 GB is Startup-4 at $75, the same plan and price as a 2 vCPU / 4 GB database.

Neon, AWS, Google Cloud, DigitalOcean, Aiven and Heroku charge no platform fee.

Sources indicate that on 15 October 2026 DigitalOcean changed its database plans. Accounts that have never created a database, and every account from 30 November, can only create Standard Edition clusters up to 4 GiB, with no standby nodes.

So a 16 GB database, or any high availability, now means Advanced Edition, from $135.75 a month. The 16 GB setup above is $283 there. The 16 GiB Standard plans still shown on the pricing page ($198.55 and $244.35) can't be bought by latest customers. If you priced DigitalOcean before mid-October, price it again.

At 1 GB, platform fees and storage minimums move the order as much as the compute price does. At 16 GB the range runs from $198 to $750, and the shape of the initiative (burstable or not, more RAM than you asked for, which edition a newly introduced account may buy) matters more than the hourly rate.

Industry observers note that I keep the full table, with every price linked to the vendor's own page, including a third size (2 vCPU, 4 GB, 50 GB) and the standby prices. Prices were checked on 9 November 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

Swapping diet drinks for water could help people lose more weight.

Women with type 2 diabetes who make the switch lose around 41 percent more weight over 18 months than those who continue drinking diet beverages.

They are also twice as likely to achieve diabetes remission during a structured weight-management programme.

The findings raise a question about whether a drink’s calorie count tells the whole story about its effects on weight.

Sweet taste without the accompanying energy might influence appetite signals.

The results suggest that everyday drink choices could play a useful supporting role in longer-term weight management.

The research involved around 80 women who were overweight or had obesity, had type 2 diabetes and regularly consumed diet drinks.

Researchers randomly assigned them either to replace their usual diet beverage with water after lunch five times a week or to continue drinking it.

Both groups took part in a six-month weight-loss programme followed by a year devoted to maintaining their progress.

By the end, women assigned to water had lost an average of 6.82 kg, compared with 4.85 kg among those continuing with diet drinks.

The difference amounted to almost 2 kg of additional weight loss across the programme.

The water group also revealed greater improvements in measures including fasting blood glucose, insulin resistance and blood fats.

Diabetes remission was reported in 90 percent of women assigned to water, compared with 45 percent of those continuing diet beverages.

According to recent reports, dr Hamid R. Farshchi, study co-author, mentioned:.

“It’s a small change with the potential for a big impact on long-term health outcomes.”.

The brain may respond differently when a sweet taste arrives without the energy normally supplied by sugar.

In a separate experiment involving around 75 adults, participants reported greater hunger after consuming sucralose than sugar, and the sweetener altered activity in the hypothalamus, a brain region involved in appetite regulation (Chakravartti et al., 2025).

However, hunger ratings after sucralose did not differ from those after water, so the findings do not establish that sweetened drinks necessarily make people hungrier than plain water.

The mismatch between sweetness and energy might help explain some appetite responses, but whether it contributed to the weight-loss difference remains unknown.

The study was published in the journal Diabetes (Farshchi Nasr et al., 2025).

Industry observers note that password Pusher creates expiring links for passwords, text, files and URLs. ZoomEye returned zero matches for app="Password Pusher" and 537 for title="Password Pusher" on 2026-11-22, using sub_type=all, page 1 and page size 1.

Industry observers note that the zero application result is a discovery limitation. The title result is the usable lead, although it can include documentation and hosted-service pages.

The matches are not confirmed deployments or exposed pushes.

The recipient uses a push link. The link may expire, allow a limited number of views, or require a passphrase. That path is intentionally available to someone outside the organization.

In a recent development, the administrator path is different. The official administration documentation describes /admin, a system-admin role and options such as two-factor authentication. The API v2 documentation describes bearer-token authentication for creating, retrieving and managing pushes.

An exposed application does not mean an exposed admin account. Review the routes separately. A public push should not provide management rights, and an API token should not be pasted into a push.

Look for owned Password Pusher deployments by title, certificate and service owner. Record the public base URL, version, authentication mode and whether the admin dashboard is reachable.

Recent findings suggest that inspect the reverse proxy rules that expose /admin, the API and public push routes. If the service is meant for a small team, restrict administration to SSO or a management network.

Review API token scope and lifetime. Remove tokens that belong to former staff or abandoned integrations. Check whether a token can manage other users or only create a push.

According to recent reports, set expiration and view limits that reflect the sensitivity of the content. A short-lived link is easier to contain than one that remains valid until someone remembers to revoke it.

Passphrases help when the link travels through a channel that may retain it. Send the link and the passphrase through different channels where possible.

Do not put secret values in application logs, analytics, browser page titles or notification previews. Review inbound email and chat scanners that may open links automatically. A scanner can consume a one-time link before the recipient does.

Alert on newly introduced administrator accounts, token creation, changes to authentication settings, repeated failed passphrase attempts and a sudden rise in push creation.

Correlate an admin login with reverse-proxy and application logs. Keep enough metadata to identify the source and route without recording the secret.

Sources indicate that the 537 title matches provide a broad candidate set. The absence of an app fingerprint means the title and page structure need manual review.

Industry observers note that state that limitation in any report. The useful question is not how many pages mention Password Pusher. It is which owned services separate public push access from administrative and API authority.

It has been revealed that nguyên tắc đơn giản nhất là bisect, giống git bisect. Đường đi của một gói tin từ máy bạn ra Internet có nhiều đoạn. Bạn đo từng đoạn một, đoạn nào tụt tốc độ thì lỗi nằm ở đó.

According to recent reports, nếu iperf3 từ laptop tới một máy khác trong LAN đã chậm thì khỏi gọi tổng đài nhà mạng, lỗi nằm trong nhà bạn. Còn nếu LAN đạt 940 Mbps (mức thực tế của Gigabit Ethernet) mà ra Internet chỉ được 200 Mbps thì lúc đó mới bắt đầu nghi router hoặc ISP.

Đây là lớp hay bị bỏ qua nhất, và cũng là lớp gây lỗi nhiều nhất. Trên Linux, ethtool (bản 6.x có sẵn trên Ubuntu 24.04) cho bạn biết NIC đang thực sự chạy ở tốc độ bao nhiêu:.

Industry observers note that trên macOS, lệnh airport -I đã bị Apple bỏ từ Sonoma. Thay vào đó bạn dùng sudo wdutil info, lệnh này cho xem RSSI, Noise, Tx Rate và channel.

Có vài pattern mình gặp đi gặp lại:.

Speedtest trên trình duyệt chỉ cho bạn một con số, và đi qua quá nhiều thành phần để biết lỗi ở đâu. iperf3 (bản 3.17+) mới là công cụ chuẩn. Bạn dựng server trên một máy trong LAN (hoặc một VPS) rồi đo từ client:.

Sources indicate that nếu LAN ổn thì chuyển sang soi đường ra Internet bằng mtr. Lệnh này kết hợp ping và traceroute, cho thấy packet loss ở từng hop:.

Recent findings suggest that chú ý một điều: một hop ở giữa hiện loss 30% nhưng các hop sau nó vẫn 0% thì thường chỉ là router đó rate-limit ICMP, không phải lỗi thật. Loss chỉ đáng lo khi nó kéo dài tới tận hop cuối.

It has been revealed that khó nhất là kiểu lỗi chỉ xuất hiện lúc 3 giờ chiều, hoặc chỉ khi đồng nghiệp bật màn hình. Muốn bắt được loại này thì phải có dữ liệu theo thời gian. Mình hay dùng script Python nhỏ dưới đây, chạy bằng cron mỗi 5 phút. Nó gọi iperf3 --json rồi ghi kết quả ra CSV:.

Cột retransmits rất đáng để ý. Throughput thấp mà retransmit cao nghĩa là đang mất gói, nên quay lại kiểm tra lớp vật lý và nhiễu. Throughput thấp mà retransmit gần 0 thì thường là bị giới hạn ở đâu đó, ví dụ QoS trên router, CPU của router bị nghẽn khi bật VPN hoặc deep packet inspection, hoặc TCP buffer quá nhỏ.

Lần tới mạng chậm, trước khi mở speedtest, bạn hãy chạy ethtool và nhìn qua mấy thiết bị USB đang cắm cạnh router.

#80621. Tech Report: WordPress Heartbeat API: The Hidden Requests That Can Slow Down Your Website

Tech Report: WordPress Heartbeat API: The Hidden Requests That Can Slow Down Your Website

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When troubleshooting a slow WordPress website, most developers start by checking plugins, themes, caching, and database queries.
  • But have you ever considered that WordPress itself might be generating repeated background requests?
  • That's exactly what I discovered while investigating a client's website.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When troubleshooting a slow WordPress website, most developers start by checking plugins, themes, caching, and database queries.

But have you ever considered that WordPress itself might be generating repeated background requests?

That's exactly what I discovered while investigating a client's website.

In my previous article, I shared how a client's WordPress website had numerous plugins installed and was experiencing performance problems.

During my investigation, I contacted the hosting provider's support team and asked them to examine the server logs.

They reported a massive number of requests associated with something called the WordPress Heartbeat API.

At the time, I wasn't familiar with Heartbeat or how it worked.

What I discovered was an crucial WordPress feature that many developers use indirectly without realizing it.

In this article, I'll explain what the WordPress Heartbeat API is, how it works, when it can affect performance, and how to investigate and control it safely.

The WordPress Heartbeat API is a built-in feature introduced in WordPress 3.6.

It allows communication between the user's browser and the WordPress server at regular intervals without requiring a full page reload.

This communication uses AJAX requests.

Heartbeat supports several vital WordPress features, including:.

For example, imagine two authors working on the same WordPress website.

When one author starts editing a post, WordPress can notify the second author that the post is already being edited.

Heartbeat helps make that communication possible.

It's a useful feature, but it also creates server requests.

Heartbeat uses JavaScript on the browser side and PHP on the server side.

The process is relatively straightforward:.

These requests commonly use the following endpoint:.

The request typically includes an action parameter:.

The notable detail is that admin-ajax.php is not exclusive to Heartbeat.

Many WordPress plugins and themes also use this endpoint for their own AJAX operations.

Therefore, seeing requests to admin-ajax.php doesn't automatically mean Heartbeat is responsible.

You need to inspect the request payload to identify the action.

Heartbeat uses a configurable interval that varies depending on the WordPress context and activity.

A commonly used default interval is around 15 seconds, although actual behavior can differ between screens and configurations.

Heartbeat can also slow its polling when browser activity changes.

This means it isn't necessarily sending requests at a fixed rate under every condition.

A single Heartbeat request usually isn't a problem.

The concern arises when many requests are generated or when processing them becomes expensive.

Suppose Heartbeat sends one request every 15 seconds.

Now imagine 10 consumers have WordPress administration pages open simultaneously.

Under those simplified assumptions, the site could receive:.

Sources indicate that these are illustrative calculations, not measurements from my client's website. Actual request counts depend on browser activity, WordPress configuration, and other factors.

Each request may require PHP processing and could trigger additional plugin callbacks.

On a server with limited resources, excessive or expensive requests can contribute to performance problems.

An administrator might have several WordPress dashboard tabs open.

If Heartbeat is active in multiple tabs, each may generate periodic requests.

Some plugins extend Heartbeat with their own functionality.

Poorly optimized callbacks can increase the amount of processing performed during a Heartbeat request.

On hosting environments with constrained CPU or PHP worker capacity, background requests can compete with other requests for resources.

However, Heartbeat requests alone don't prove the cause of a performance matter.

They are a signal worth investigating.

You don't necessarily need a performance plugin to inspect Heartbeat activity.

Your browser's developer tools are a useful starting point.

Leave the page open long enough to observe whether requests repeat.

Click a request and inspect its payload.

If you see that action, you've identified a Heartbeat request.

You can also inspect the request's timing and response.

Remember that the total request duration isn't the same as PHP execution time, and a slow request doesn't necessarily mean Heartbeat itself is inefficient.

Browser DevTools show requests from your own browser session.

Server logs can help reveal request patterns across the website.

You can ask your hosting provider to investigate:.

This is exactly why contacting hosting support was valuable in my client's case.

The logs gave me a technical lead that wasn't obvious from looking at the website.

Once you've confirmed that Heartbeat activity deserves investigation, you can consider adjusting its behavior.

However, I wouldn't recommend disabling it globally as a first step.

Heartbeat supports useful functionality, and changing it can affect the editing experience.

WordPress provides the heartbeat_settings filter, which lets developers modify Heartbeat settings.

This example sets the polling interval to 60 seconds.

You can place the code in a small custom plugin or another appropriate location where your WordPress customizations are managed.

The interval is subject to WordPress's supported limits, and the effective polling behavior may vary depending on the page and activity.

Vital: Increasing the interval reduces polling frequency, but it also means Heartbeat-dependent updates may take longer.

Always test the affected functionality.

Rather than changing the interval everywhere, you can apply a different setting on a particular administration screen.

This example targets the main WordPress dashboard screen.

It doesn't globally disable Heartbeat or change the post editor's interval.

Screen-specific changes can be preferable when you've identified a particular area that needs adjustment.

WordPress also provides a way to dequeue scripts.

This example attempts to remove Heartbeat from the main dashboard page.

It should only be used after confirming that no required functionality on that screen depends on Heartbeat.

I would avoid disabling Heartbeat throughout the administration area, especially in the post editor, without understanding the consequences.

My preference is to investigate and make targeted adjustments rather than disabling core functionality blindly.

After changing Heartbeat settings, return to the browser's Network tab.

Check whether the frequency of Heartbeat requests has changed as expected.

Then test important WordPress functionality.

Ideally, compare measurements before and after the change under similar conditions.

If you have access to server monitoring, look at PHP worker utilization, CPU activity, and request volume.

A reduction in Heartbeat requests doesn't automatically prove that the website became faster.

The objective is to determine whether the change improved the original problem without introducing new problems.

When the hosting provider first mentioned WordPress Heartbeat, I didn't know much about it.

I had worked with WordPress for years, but this particular feature wasn't something I had previously needed to investigate in detail.

The experience reminded me of three vital lessons.

Looking at the website's frontend doesn't always reveal what is happening on the server.

Logs and resource metrics can provide valuable evidence.

Plugins can be useful, but adding one without understanding the problem can make the setup more complicated.

Sometimes WordPress already provides the hooks and tools needed to investigate or adjust a feature.

What matters is the ability to investigate unfamiliar behavior, understand the underlying system, and evaluate possible solutions.

In my case, a real client problem motivated me to learn about a WordPress feature I hadn't previously explored.

And that knowledge became useful beyond the original project.

One final point worth mentioning is that Heartbeat and WP-Cron are different mechanisms.

Both are worth understanding when troubleshooting WordPress performance, but they should not be confused.

In my next article, I'll explore WP-Cron in more detail, including how it works, why scheduled tasks sometimes fail or run late, and when using a real server cron job can be useful.

The WordPress Heartbeat API is not a bug or an unnecessary feature.

It provides useful functionality that helps WordPress deliver a better editing and administration experience.

However, like any server-side activity, it can contribute to performance problems under certain conditions.

The key is understanding how it works, measuring its impact, and making changes only when the evidence supports them.

My experience with a client's website taught me that troubleshooting isn't always about finding a latest tool.

Sometimes it's about discovering a feature you didn't know existed.

Before disabling Heartbeat or installing another optimization plugin, investigate the requests and understand what's actually happening.

llama.cpp server now ships with router mode, which lets you dynamically load, unload, and switch between multiple models without restarting.

Reminder: llama.cpp server is a lightweight, OpenAI-compatible HTTP server for running LLMs locally.

Recent findings suggest that this feature was a popular request to bring Ollama-style model management to llama.cpp. It uses a multi-process architecture where each model runs in its own process, so if one model crashes, others remain unaffected.

Start the server in router mode by not specifying a model:.

This auto-discovers models from your llama.cpp cache (LLAMA_CACHE or ~/.cache/llama.cpp). If you've previously downloaded models via llama-server -hf user/model, they'll be available automatically.

You can also point to a local directory of GGUF files:.

According to recent reports, on the first request, the server automatically loads the model into memory (loading time depends on model size). Subsequent requests to the same model are instant since it's already loaded.

Returns all discovered models with their status (loaded, loading, or unloaded).

All model instances inherit settings from the router:.

All loaded models will use 8192 context and full GPU offload. You can also define per-model settings using presets:.

The built-in web UI also supports model switching. Just select a model from the dropdown and it loads automatically.

We hope this feature makes it easier to A/B test different model versions, run multi-tenant deployments, or simply switch models during development without restarting the server.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

When people in decades-long marriages describe what helped them through a crisis, most of the responses they give involve leaning on each other.

They describe listening to each other, talking through painful subjects and sometimes having the same argument more than once.

The researchers suggest that this response grows out of years of knowing they can count on their partner.

In attachment theory, a partner can act as a safe haven, someone whose presence makes it easier to bear distress.

Getting through a difficult period together may deepen that trust, making it easier to ask for help the next time it is needed.

Dr Christian Heim, the study’s first author, and Dr Caroline Heim, study co-author, interviewed each couple together, asking each person to describe what had put their marriage under strain and what had helped them cope.

The 180 participants were born in 24 countries and, with a few exceptions, had been married for at least 40 years.

Around two-thirds of the couples described a threat they believed could have ended their marriage, such as the death or serious illness of a child, infidelity or prolonged periods apart.

Talking, listening and arguing accounted for almost a quarter of the coping responses the researchers recorded.

After an affair, some couples described arguing over it repeatedly, while bereaved partners sometimes waited for a moment when both felt able to speak.

One partner in an American couple married for 45 years recalled asking their spouse about the son they had lost.

“Can I talk about our son? I’m hurting. Is it okay to talk about it?”.

Some partners described taking time to grieve separately before they were ready to turn to each other.

Around four in five coping responses involved leaning on the relationship, whether by drawing closer, persevering as a couple or giving up something one partner wanted.

The interviews capture what couples in lasting marriages felt had helped them, leaving open whether the same approaches would have helped couples who separated.

When partners see a problem as something they face together, they may spend less time working out who is to blame and more time trying to understand what the other person is going through.

A previous analysis involving almost 18,000 people found that coping together and helping a partner manage stress were both linked to greater relationship satisfaction (Falconier et al., 2015).

Some couples in the interviews felt that an illness, a bereavement or a family conflict had left them closer, even though the experience itself had been painful.

A British couple married for 60 years described how they got through a serious conflict with their in-laws:.

The study was published in the journal The American Journal of Family Therapy (Heim & Heim, 2025).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI agents are rapidly becoming essential for building intelligent applications, but creating robust, adaptable agents that scale across domains remains a challenge.
  • CUGA (Configurable Generalist Agent) was designed to overcome these limitations.
  • Recent findings suggest that CUGA is a configurable, general-purpose AI agent that supports complex, multi-step tasks across web and API environments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI agents are rapidly becoming essential for building intelligent applications, but creating robust, adaptable agents that scale across domains remains a challenge. Many existing frameworks struggle with brittleness, tool misuse, and failures when faced with complex workflows.

CUGA (Configurable Generalist Agent) was designed to overcome these limitations. It's an open-source, AI Agent that combines flexibility, reliability, and ease of use for enterprise use cases. By abstracting orchestration complexity, CUGA empowers developers to focus on domain requirements rather than the internals of agent building. And now, with its integration into 🚀Hugging Face Spaces🚀, experimenting with CUGA and open models has never been easier.

Recent findings suggest that CUGA is a configurable, general-purpose AI agent that supports complex, multi-step tasks across web and API environments. It has achieved state-of-the-art performance on leading benchmarks:.

🥇 #1 on AppWorld - a benchmark with 750 real-world tasks across 457 APIs.

🥈 Top-tier on WebArena (#1 from 02/25 - 09/25) - showcases CUGA Computer Use capabilities with a complex benchmark for autonomous web agents across application domains.

We're also continuing to innovate with fresh experimental capabilities, including:.

Figure 1: CUGA Agentic Architecture.

In a recent development, the CUGA architecture begins with the user's message flowing into a chat layer that interprets intent and constructs the user's goal, based on context. A task planning and control component then decomposes this goal into structured subtasks, tracked programmatically through a dynamic task ledger. This ledger supports re-planning when needed, ensuring robust execution. Subtasks are delegated to specialized agents, such as the API agent, which uses an inner reasoning loop to generate pseudo-code instructions before invoking code in a secure sandbox. The system leverages a tool registry that goes beyond MCP protocols to parse and understand tool capabilities, enabling precise orchestration. Once all steps are completed, the final response is returned to the user, delivering reliable, policy-aligned outcomes.

CUGA works best when inference is fast. When each call takes seconds, delays compound and force a tradeoff between agent capability and user experience. Running on high-performance inference platforms like Groq indicates how fast inference fundamentally expands what agent architectures can achieve.

CUGA is fully open source, under the Apache 2.0 license, and you can find us at cuga.dev.

By embracing open models, CUGA aligns with the Hugging Face ethos of democratizing AI-giving developers the freedom to choose models that best fit their needs, whether for experimentation or production.

It has been revealed that CUGA has been tested with a variety of open models, including gpt-oss-120b and Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct-fp8 (both hosted on Groq). Our Hugging Face Space uses gpt-oss-120b, with the model hosted on Groq, offering a rapid response time for LLM calls.

According to recent reports, groq runs open models on its custom‑built LPUs, which are designed for AI inference and optimal for repeated agent inferences required by CUGA's architecture, enabling planning, execution, and validation steps to finish fast. The result is strong cost and performance: open models are ~80-90% cheaper than closed alternatives; Groq's OpenAI-compatible APIs meet production latency needs, and CUGA stays fully configurable across models, providers, and deployment topologies.

To make agent development even more accessible, CUGA integrates with Langflow, an open-source visual programming interface for building LLM-powered workflows. Its intuitive drag-and-drop interface reduces the barrier to entry for those who prefer low-code solutions.

Starting with Langflow 1.7.0, CUGA ships with its own widget, enabling consumers to assemble complex, multi-tool agents visually and deploy with a click. Give it a try at langflow.org.

We've launched a CUGA demo on Hugging Face Spaces to give you a taste of what's possible. This demo showcases a small CRM system and equips CUGA with 20 preconfigured tools for handling sales related data queries and API interactions through the API Agent. To make experimentation even more powerful, the demo provides access to workspace files, enabling you to use predefined policies.

Give it a try on Hugging Face Spaces and share your feedback!

Industry observers note that CUGA brings a fresh level of flexibility and openness to AI agent building. To engage with us:.

Impressive work on CUGA’s architecture and configurability. The structured planning, tool orchestration, and benchmark results demonstrate a strong approach to scalable agent design. Integration with Hugging Face Spaces and Langflow significantly lowers the barrier to experimentation and deployment.Here is our Website: https://www.simbainstitute.in/artificial-intelligence-course-in-surat/.

#80615. Duplicate refunds from scattered status checks: fixing it with the State pattern in C#

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (898 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Duplicate refunds from scattered status checks: fixing it with the State pattern in C#

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This post was originally published in Portuguese on my blog: Status de pedido com if espalhado gera estorno duplo -> State.
  • Every order system has an Order class with a Status property.
  • It has been revealed that the order goes through Pending, Paid, Shipped and Delivered, and it can be cancelled before shipping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This post was originally published in Portuguese on my blog: Status de pedido com if espalhado gera estorno duplo -> State.

Every order system has an Order class with a Status property. At first there are three or four statuses, each action checks the current status with an if, and everything is fine. The trouble indicates up months later, when a latest status arrives and nobody remembers all the places that needed to know about it. In this post I'll show a very concrete case of that, a refund paid twice, and how the State pattern solves it without ceremony.

It has been revealed that the order goes through Pending, Paid, Shipped and Delivered, and it can be cancelled before shipping. If it was already paid, cancelling issues a refund. The Cancel() method in the "before" version is the kind of code everyone has written:.

Look at the first condition: it's a list of what is not allowed. And the second one assumes that anything that isn't Pending has been paid. As long as the enum had only those statuses, both assumptions were true.

Then the business asked for returns. Someone created the Returned status and the fresh method, with a refund:.

Return() is correct. The bug is in Cancel(), which nobody opened: Returned isn't in the forbidden list and isn't Pending, so a returned order can be cancelled and the customer gets refunded a second time. No test broke, because the existing tests didn't know Returned existed. In the project I left a test, Cancelling_a_returned_order_refunds_twice, that documents exactly this behavior in the old version.

That's the real pain of the status-based if: each status's rules end up scattered across every method. To add a status you have to review every action, and the compiler doesn't warn you about any of them.

Sources indicate that the idea is to flip the question. Instead of every action asking "what status am I in?", each status becomes a class that knows which actions it accepts. The order only holds the current state and delegates to it. The base class forbids everything by default:.

It has been revealed that this "forbidden by default" is the most important point of the design. A fresh state is born with no permissions at all, and you explicitly allow what makes sense. It's the opposite of the old Cancel()'s forbidden list.

Each state overrides only what it allows and returns the next state. The refund for a cancellation lives where it makes sense, in PaidState:.

The Order class in the "after" version became trivial: a _state field that starts as PendingState, and each action is a one-liner like public void Cancel() => _state = _state.Cancel(this);. The refund is done by IssueRefund(), marked internal so that only the states, in the same assembly, can call it.

Sources indicate that and ReturnedState? It only declares its own Status. It doesn't override Cancel, so cancelling a returned order throws InvalidOperationException with "Cannot cancel an order that is Returned." without anyone having to remember it.

First, the bug goes away by construction, not by discipline. The Cancelling_a_returned_order_is_rejected test checks that the cancellation is refused, that the status stays Returned and that RefundCount stays at 1.

Second, reading the code changes. To know what a paid order can do, you open PaidState and everything is there, in a few lines. In the old version you had to read the five methods of Order and assemble the state machine in your head.

It has been revealed that third, extension becomes local. A fresh status, like "being picked" or "awaiting pickup", is a new class plus a tweak to the state that leads to it. The other states aren't touched. Tests also get more direct: each transition has a short test, and refusals are tested by the exception message.

State has a cost, and it's not a small one. You trade one file for several, and whoever arrives at the code has to understand the pattern before finding where each rule lives. For a three-status flow that never changes, a well-written switch is more honest and easier to read.

It also isn't worth it when the transitions are basically data, with no behavior: if all you need is "from A you can go to B or C", a transition table (a dictionary, or even a database table) solves it with less code and lets you change it without a deploy. State shines when each transition carries its own behavior, like the refund here, sending an email or reserving stock.

It has been revealed that another thing to watch is persistence. In the database you keep storing the Status enum, and when loading the order you need to rebuild the state object from it. It's a simple mapping, but it's one more piece to maintain. And if the states start accumulating dependencies (repositories, payment gateways), stop and think: maybe the rule belongs in an application service, and the state should only say whether the transition is allowed.

My rule of thumb: if you've already fixed a bug because of a status forgotten in some if, or if the status enum got its fifth value, State is worth considering.

The project has both versions side by side, in the Before and After folders, with tests for each. All you need is Docker installed:.

The full code is on GitHub: programero-csharp/2026-11-order-status-state-pattern.

spov: OpenCode in disposable Modal sandboxes

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (727 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I wanted to run OpenCode in Modal sandboxes.
  • It has been revealed that I'm betting on open source to keep winning in the longer run when it comes to developer tooling, even in the agentic era.
  • Anyway, what I also developed was a wish for an easy way to kick off agent sessions in sandboxed environments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I wanted to run OpenCode in Modal sandboxes. Then I wanted better support for larger one-shot jobs. And then I wanted a web UI. It resulted in spov: at its core, a simple Modal sandbox for headless OpenCode sessions, with an optional job runner and web control pane.

It has been revealed that I'm betting on open source to keep winning in the longer run when it comes to developer tooling, even in the agentic era. I love open and customizable OSS harnesses like Pi and OpenCode; the transparency and extensibility they bring is very much something I want from my local development tooling.

Anyway, what I also developed was a wish for an easy way to kick off agent sessions in sandboxed environments. And I've been using Modal's services for some side project experimentation and model training in the past, which made me aware both of their free tier with $30 of credits a month and of their pretty convenient APIs. All in all, it's an easy platform to integrate with. It's focused and opinionated, and seemingly pretty robust too.

Recent findings suggest that so the choice landed on OpenCode + Modal. In its simplest form, you cd into a repo and run spov fly. You get the standard OpenCode TUI in your terminal, but the OpenCode server runs in a fresh Modal sandbox with only the repositories you chose. When you quit, the agent's commits and changes are synced back to your local checkout.

There are other projects operating in this area, with slightly different ambitions and scopes. Some examples:.

What I was looking for is a bit different: Something I can start from my terminal in the normal OpenCode TUI, when I prefer to, and get the work back on my branch. But I also need it to be capable of working in a more remote-first mode, pulling remotes and pushing back work as PRs to the remote. Another piece on the wish list was: No real token or key inside the sandbox at all. They stay in a proxy beside it, and the agent only sees placeholders (in all three above, the agent's environment holds real credentials).

I wouldn't say it's impossible that I will open up for more plug-and-play sandbox providers in spov, even if I don't have any intentions of supporting anything other than Modal at the moment. But when it comes to agent harness support, it's very unlikely that spov will ever try to become a multi-harness environment. It started out as a very thin launcher and wrapper around OpenCode, and there's a strength in leaning into some of OpenCode's mechanisms rather than going fully generic.

Industry observers note that A lot of tooling in this space assumes your code lives on GitHub. Mine mostly does too, but I didn't want spov to lock in too hard to GitHub. So spov supports GitHub, Forgejo and Gitea (Codeberg, Codefloe or your own instance), and GitLab works as well. A sandbox can clone from and push to any of them, and a job can end in a pull request on whichever forge the repo lives on. Inside the sandbox, the agent gets the forge's own CLI (gh, tea or glab), but never the real token: that stays in the credential proxy, same as the model keys.

In a recent development, gitHub, Codefloe (Forgejo) and gitlab.com are tested end to end against real sandboxes, and Forgejo and Gitea also run in CI. If you're on a self-hosted forge and something doesn't work, do reach out!

Sources indicate that spov is a personal side project, free and open source under the MIT license, and there's no commercial angle to it. That also means there's no fully managed or hosted version at the moment. Local mode needs no setup at all though: the CLI starts its own small server. For jobs and the dashboard, you run spov serve with Postgres on your own infrastructure (there's a Compose file in the repo), and the dashboard signs in with GitHub.

If a hosted version is something you'd want, please reach out or open a feature request on GitHub. Knowing that there's interest is what would make me consider it.

I'm using it for some personal projects, but I'm open-sourcing it in case someone happens to have the exact same preferences and needs ;-).

Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers

📅 09 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1233 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more.
  • Multimodal embedding models map inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space, while multimodal reranker models score the relevance of mixed-modality pairs.
  • If you want to train your own multimodal models, check out the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. With the v5.4 update, you can now encode and compare texts, images, audio, and videos using the same familiar API. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use these upcoming multimodal capabilities for both embedding and reranking.

Multimodal embedding models map inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space, while multimodal reranker models score the relevance of mixed-modality pairs. This opens up use cases like visual document retrieval, cross-modal search, and multimodal RAG pipelines.

If you want to train your own multimodal models, check out the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

According to recent reports, traditional embedding models convert text into fixed-size vectors. Multimodal embedding models extend this by mapping inputs from different modalities (text, images, audio, or video) into a shared embedding space. This means you can compare a text query against image documents (or vice versa) using the same similarity functions you're already familiar with.

It has been revealed that similarly, traditional reranker (Cross Encoder) models compute relevance scores between pairs of texts. Multimodal rerankers can score pairs where one or both elements are images, combined text-image documents, or other modalities.

For example, you can compare a text query against image documents, find video clips matching a description, or build RAG pipelines that work across modalities.

Multimodal models require some extra dependencies. Install the extras for the modalities you need (see Installation for more details):.

Sources indicate that VLM-based models like Qwen3-VL-2B require a GPU with at least ~8 GB of VRAM. For the 8B variants, expect ~20 GB. If you don't have a local GPU, consider using a cloud GPU service or Google Colab. On CPU, these models will be extremely slow; text-only or CLIP models are better suited for CPU inference.

Loading a multimodal embedding model works exactly like loading a text-only model:.

Recent findings suggest that some models might require a revision argument for now if the integration pull requests for the model is still pending. Once they're merged, you'll be able to load them without specifying a revision, like above.

In a recent development, the model automatically detects which modalities it supports, so there's nothing extra to configure. See Processor and Model kwargs if you want to control things like image resolution or model precision.

With a multimodal model loaded, model.encode() accepts images alongside text. Images can be provided as URLs, local file paths, or PIL Image objects (see Supported Input Types for all accepted formats):.

You can compute similarities between text embeddings and image embeddings, since the model maps both into the same space:.

In a recent development, as expected, "A green car parked in front of a yellow building" is most similar to the car image (0.51), and "A bee on a pink flower" is most similar to the bee image (0.67). The hard negatives ("A red car driving on a highway", "A wasp on a wooden table") correctly receive lower scores.

You might notice that even the best matching scores (0.51, 0.67) aren't very close to 1.0. This is due to the modality gap: embeddings from different modalities tend to cluster in separate regions of the space. Cross-modal similarities are typically lower than within-modal ones (e.g., text-to-text), but the relative ordering is preserved, so retrieval still works well.

For retrieval tasks, encode_query() and encode_document() are the recommended methods. Many retrieval models prepend different instruction prompts depending on whether the input is a query or a document, similar to how chat models might apply different system prompts depending on the goal. Model authors can specify their prompts in the model config, and encode_query() / encode_document() automatically load and apply the correct one:.

Under the hood, both are thin wrappers around encode(), they just handle prompt selection for you. Here's what cross-modal retrieval looks like:.

Recent findings suggest that these methods accept the same input types as encode() (images, URLs, multimodal dicts, etc.) and pass through the same parameters. For models without specialized query/document prompts, they behave identically to encode().

Multimodal reranker (CrossEncoder) models score the relevance between pairs of inputs, where each element can be text, an image, audio, video, or a combination. They tend to outperform embedding models in terms of quality, but are slower since they process each pair individually. The currently available pretrained multimodal rerankers focus on text and image inputs, but the architecture supports any modality that the underlying model can handle.

The rank() method scores and ranks a list of documents against a query, supporting mixed modalities:.

According to recent reports, the reranker correctly identifies the car image (document 0) as the most relevant result, followed by the combined text+image document about a car in a European city (document 3). The bee image (document 1) scores lowest. Keep in mind that the modality gap can influence absolute scores: text-image pair scores may occupy a different range than text-text or image-image pair scores.

You can also check which modalities a reranker supports using modalities and supports(), just like with embedding models:.

You can also use predict() to get raw relevance scores for specific pairs of inputs:.

A common pattern is to use an embedding model for fast initial retrieval, then refine the top results with a reranker:.

In a recent development, since the corpus embeddings are pre-computed, the initial retrieval is fast even over millions of documents. The reranker then provides more accurate scoring over the smaller candidate set.

In a recent development, multimodal models accept a variety of input formats. Here's a summary of what you can pass to model.encode():.

You can check which modalities a model supports using the modalities property and supports() method:.

Industry observers note that the "message" modality indicates that the model accepts chat-style message inputs with interleaved content. In practice, you rarely need to use this directly. When you pass strings, URLs, or multimodal dicts, the model converts them to the appropriate message format internally. Sentence Transformers supports two message formats:.

The format is auto-detected from the model's chat template.

Since all inputs get converted into the same message format internally, you can mix input types in a single encode() call:.

If a model doesn't follow either format and you need full control, you can pass raw message dicts with role and content keys directly:.

This bypasses the automatic format conversion and passes the messages directly to the processor's apply_chat_template().

It has been revealed that you may want to control image resolution bounds or model precision. Use processor_kwargs and model_kwargs when loading the model:.

See the SentenceTransformer API Reference documentation for more details on these kwargs.

In Sentence Transformers v5.4, tokenizer_kwargs has been renamed to processor_kwargs to reflect that multimodal models use processors rather than just tokenizers. The old name is still accepted but deprecated.

Here are the multimodal models supported in v5.4, also available in the v5.4 integrations collection:.

The older CLIP models continue to be supported:.

These simple CLIP models still work well on lower-resource hardware.

To learn how to finetune these multimodal models on your own data, see the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

The training companion to this post and adjacent Sentence Transformers guides:.
