Nvidia without Jensen Huang: the resignation, the earnings and the GPU/CUDA concentration risk

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This post was originally published in Portuguese on my blog: Nvidia sem Jensen Huang: renúncia, balanço e risco de concentração em GPU/CUDA.
  • In 33 years of history, Nvidia has had only one CEO.
  • The official announcement gives no reason.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This post was originally published in Portuguese on my blog: Nvidia sem Jensen Huang: renúncia, balanço e risco de concentração em GPU/CUDA.

In 33 years of history, Nvidia has had only one CEO. Last Thursday, November 12, that ended: Jensen Huang resigned as chairman, CEO and board member, effective immediately. The CFO, Colette Kress, took over as interim CEO while the board searches for a successor. Harvey Jones, on the board since 1993, became the first chair of the board in the manufacturer's history.

The official announcement gives no reason. What is known comes from the press. The New York Times and the Financial Times reported in the previous weeks that Huang had a relationship with an executive who, according to the reports, was the target of a Chinese intelligence operation, and the board hired an independent investigation. The day before the resignation, the New York Times added that there was a second relationship, with a vice president who reported directly to him, and the Wall Street Journal said the board was preparing to remove him. Nvidia didn't confirm these reports, so it's worth treating them as reporting, not settled fact.

It has been revealed that the stock fell more than 10% at the open that day. Five days later, Nvidia released results for the quarter ended in October, the first without Huang: revenue of US$ 115.8 billion, up 103% year over year, with US$ 107.6 billion coming from data center. Guidance for the next quarter is US$ 130 billion, without counting any data center compute sales to China. In other words, the machine keeps running.

According to recent reports, first, the obvious: nothing breaks today. CUDA still compiles, the published product roadmap still stands, and the Rubin platform is already shipping. Analysts quoted in the press say much of the next two years is already contracted and designed. If your training and inference pipeline is stable, the CEO's resignation is no reason to touch it.

The more interesting point is a different one. Analysts described Nvidia as a manufacturer built around one person, with no named successor, where many decisions about pace and priorities went through him. That matters because almost everyone building AI today depends on this company: clouds, startups, in-house data teams. A consultancy cited by CIO recommended exactly this to technology leaders: don't overreact, but use the moment to review concentration risk in AI infrastructure suppliers.

In a recent development, for developers, the message is more concrete. According to Nvidia's own annual report, more than 7.5 million developers use CUDA and its tools. It's a huge ecosystem, and that coupling is exactly what makes switching vendors expensive. I see no reason to migrate anything because of a governance crisis. But I do see a reason to ask a question almost nobody asks until they have to: if tomorrow I had to run this on other hardware, how much of my code is glued to a specific API and how much sits behind a layer I control? Finding out the answer costs an afternoon. Finding out at the wrong time costs a quarter.

Recent findings suggest that there's a parallel with our day-to-day that seems more useful to me than the gossip. Every team knows the bus factor, that person who, if they leave, takes with them the knowledge nobody documented. Nvidia is worth trillions and had the same problem, just at industry scale. The successor most cited by analysts is Ian Buck, the engineer who helped create CUDA and now runs the data center business, and other outside names, like Arm's CEO, show up on the lists. If the pick is a technical profile from inside, the roadmap should stay as it is. If someone comes from outside, the conversation changes.

I also think the story has an uncomfortable side for the whole industry: an executive's personal life became a national security issue and an AI supply chain issue at the same time. When a technology's infrastructure depends this much on one firm, any fragility of theirs becomes everyone's fragility. It's worth watching the succession process over the next few weeks, because it will say more about the platform's future than any headline about the resignation.

Granite 4.1 LLMs: How They’re Built

📅 29 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1711 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.
  • According to recent reports, TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens.
  • It has been revealed that building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.

According to recent reports, TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens. The models are further refined with supervised fine‑tuning on ~4.1M high‑quality curated samples and reinforcement learning via on‑policy GRPO with DAPO loss (Yu et al., 2025). Notably, the 8B instruct model matches or surpasses the previous Granite 4.0‑H‑Small (32B‑A9B MoE) despite using a simpler dense architecture with fewer parameters. All Granite 4.1 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

It has been revealed that building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training. For Granite 4.1, we prioritized data quality over quantity, progressively refining the data mixture across five pre‑training stages. We further curated supervised fine‑tuning data using an LLM‑as‑Judge framework and applied a multi‑stage reinforcement learning pipeline to systematically strengthen performance in math, coding, instruction following, and general chat.

Granite 4.1 models use a decoder-only dense transformer architecture. The core design choices include Grouped Query Attention (GQA), Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), SwiGLU activations, RMSNorm, and shared input/output embeddings.

All three model sizes share the same training pipeline and data strategy, differing only in architecture dimensions.

Granite 4.1 is trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five‑phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre‑training, phases 3–4 perform mid‑training with progressively higher‑quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long‑context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase employs a distinct data mixture and learning‑rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web‑scale data to more curated, domain‑specific content.

Figure 2: The five-phase pre-training pipeline. Phases 1–2 are pre-training, Phases 3–4 are mid-training (high-quality data annealing), and Phase 5 is long context training (LCE).

The first phase establishes broad language understanding using a general mixture of training data with a power learning rate schedule and warmup.

Phase 2 sharply increases the proportion of code and mathematical data, pivoting toward stronger reasoning capabilities while still maintaining general language coverage.

In a recent development, phase 3 transitions into mid-training with a more balanced, high-quality mixture and an exponential decay learning rate schedule. This is where we start blending in chain-of-thought and synthetic instruction data.

The fourth phase continues mid-training with a linear learning rate decay to zero, focusing the model on the highest-quality data available.

Figure 3: How the data mix evolves across the pre-training phases. Notice the progressive shift from web-heavy (Phase 1) to quality-heavy with instruction and reasoning data (Phases 3–4).

The fifth and final phase also part of of mid-training extends the context window from 4K to 512K through a staged long-context extension process:.

It has been revealed that the LCE phase uses an exponential learning rate schedule starting at 1e-4 and decaying to 0. To ensure the model natively handles long sequences without degrading short-context performance, we do a model merge after each LCE stage. RULER benchmark of base models:.

According to recent reports, supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) is what turns the base model into a reliable instruction‑following assistant, making data quality critically important—since even a small number of incorrect or hallucinated samples can instill undesirable behaviors. To address this, we apply a rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework alongside rule‑based filtering to curate high-quality samples. Together, the pipeline automatically assess each sample against structural, semantic, and behavioral criteria, fixing concerns when possible and filtering out samples that fail to meet our quality standards.

Figure 4: The SFT data quality pipeline. Raw conversation data passes through an LLM-as-Judge with a multi-dimensional rubric, producing accept/borderline/reject verdicts. Hard-reject defects (hallucination, false premise, incorrect computation) trigger automatic rejection regardless of score.

It has been revealed that our rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework evaluates only assistant responses, treating system prompts, user inputs, retrieved documents, and tool outputs strictly as contextual information. This ensures that the judge assesses what the model indicates, rather than what it was asked to do. In RAG settings, responses that are not grounded in the retrieved context are flagged as hallucinations, while tool‑use outputs are validated against the set of allowed tools and their parameter schemas.

Industry observers note that we employ specialized judge prompts tailored to different SFT data types, including multi‑turn dialogue, RAG‑augmented responses, tool‑calling interactions, and multilingual conversations. Each response is scored across six weighted dimensions—instruction following, correctness, completeness, conciseness, naturalness, and calibration (with optional critical‑thinking checks). Samples are accepted, flagged as borderline, or rejected based on deterministic score thresholds, with hard‑reject rules overriding scores for severe defects such as hallucinations, false premises, or incorrect computations.

To complement semantic evaluation, we apply a deterministic rule‑based pipeline that enforces structural integrity through text normalization, truncation and length filtering, schema validation, and leakage detection. A final global deduplication step ensures dataset‑wide uniqueness. All filtering and correction actions are fully auditable.

After passing through the LLM-as-Judge, rule-based filtering, and global deduplication pipeline, we fine-tune base models on these approximately 4.1 million high-quality samples. The following details apply to all three model variants:.

According to recent reports, after SFT, we apply a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline to further improve the model's capabilities across specific domains. Rather than a single RL pass, we run multiple targeted RL stages, each optimizing for different capabilities.

We use On-policy GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) (Shao et al., 2024) with DAPO (Decoupled Clip and Dynamic sAmpling Policy Optimization) loss (Yu et al., 2025) which provides more stable training signals compared to standard GRPO. However, due to computationally intensive nature of dynamic sampling, we switch it off during our training runs.

Figure 10 depicts our Reinforcement Learning pipeline for training Granite 4.1 models. Through extensive experimentation with a variety of reinforcement learning recipes, we found that this sequence of steps minimizes catastrophic forgetting while simultaneously maximizing performance across multiple domains.

Figure 10: The Granite 4.1 reinforcement learning pipeline consisting of four sequential stages: Multi-domain RL, RLHF, Identity and Knowledge-calibration RL, and Math RL.

Industry observers note that in this stage, the model is trained jointly on a unified mixture of data drawn from multiple domains. Every gradient patch therefore reflects the full diversity of tasks, which prevents catastrophic forgetting, boosts overall benchmark performance, and minimizes regressions on any individual task.

The different domains covered in this stage include:.

During this stage, we trained the models on 45,504 unique prompts (averaged across all Granite 4.1 models) and found that a learning rate of 5e‑7 with a KL‑loss coefficient ($\beta$) of 0.05 performed best for multi‑domain reinforcement learning.

Industry observers note that to further improve the model's helpfulness and chat ability, we train our model on generic-chat prompts using a multilingual scalar reward model. With this stage, we observed an average improvement of ~18.9 points (averaged across the three Granite 4.1 models) in Alpaca-Eval compared to the SFT checkpoints.

Recent findings suggest that to mitigate policy drift from its previously learned knowledge, we use a conservative learning rate of 3e-7 and higher KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09 in this stage. We use an average of 17,920 unique prompts in this RLHF stage.

Sources indicate that in this stage, we train the model for a few steps (~40 training steps) on identity and knowledge calibration prompts. We observed that this small training stage significantly improves the model's self-identification capabilities.

Similar to the RLHF stage, we used a learning rate of 3e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09, and we use 1728 unique prompts in this stage.

During our RL training, we found that the RLHF stage causes a drop in math benchmark scores (e.g., in GSM8K, DeepMind-Math). The Math RL stage enables the model to recover from this drop and surpasses the original SFT performance on math benchmarks: ~3.8 points on average for GSM8K, and ~23.48 points on average for DeepMind-Math. We use an average of 13,504 unique prompts in this stage and similar to the multi-domain RL stage, we used a learning rate of 5e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.05.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

Granite 4.1 delivers competitive instruction‑following and tool‑calling capabilities without relying on long chains of thought. By avoiding extended reasoning traces, it provides predictable latency, stable token usage, and lower operational cost. This makes Granite 4.1 a production‑ready, open‑source choice for enterprise workloads where efficiency, reliability, and cost control are critical.

A striking result: the Granite 4.1-8B dense model consistently matches or outperforms the previous-generation Granite 4.0-H-Small, a 32B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 9B active parameters.

In a recent development, figure 13: Granite 4.1-8B (dark blue) vs. Granite 4.0-H-Small 32B-A9B (light blue) across benchmarks. The 8B dense model matches or exceeds the larger MoE model on IFEval, AlpacaEval, MMLU-Pro, BBH, GSM8K, DeepMind-Math, Evalplus, ArenaHard, BFCL V3 and MBPP(+).

Figure 14: Comparison across the Granite 4.1 family — 30B, 8B, and 3B models. Scores scale predictably with model size, with the 30B model leading across all benchmarks.

According to recent reports, we also released fp8 quantized variants of the Granite 4.1 models, optimized for inference with vLLM. The precision is reduced from 16‑bit to 8‑bit, resulting in approximately a 50% reduction in both disk footprint and GPU memory usage. Quantization is applied only to the weights and activations of linear operators within the transformer blocks using LLM Compressor, while all other layers are preserved at their original precision.

We trained the Granite 4.1 Language Models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted on CoreWeave:.

This infrastructure provides the scalable, high-bandwidth interconnect needed for efficient distributed training at the token volumes required (15T+ tokens across pre-training alone).

Granite 4.1 models are available under the Apache 2.0 license. Here's how to get started with the 30B instruct model wiht tool calling example:.

Granite 4.1 marks a significant step forward for high‑quality, open‑source language models. By prioritizing data quality and rigor at every stage—from pre‑training curation to supervised fine‑tuning and multi‑stage reinforcement learning—we deliver a substantially improved post‑training pipeline. The result is stronger instruction following, tool use, and conversational performance, showing that carefully trained dense 8B models can rival much larger MoE architectures. We’re excited to see how the community adopts and builds on these models.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.

One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.

Track pants, also known as tracksuit bottoms, receive the lower ratings for perceived intelligence compared with blouses, ordinary trousers or long skirts in a study of women’s clothing.

Of the six types of clothing the researchers compared, track pants also received the lowest average ratings for trustworthiness.

Blouses topped the rankings for intelligence and trustworthiness but scored near the bottom for confidence.

Short skirts highlighted almost the reverse pattern, scoring near the top for confidence and lower than long skirts on both intelligence and trustworthiness.

Short skirts also gave the strongest impression of sexual interest, showing how much people can read into a hemline.

Long skirts fell between short skirts and blouses on confidence, while ordinary trousers scored higher than tracksuit bottoms on both intelligence and trustworthiness.

Onesies gave the strongest impression of happiness and scored about as high as short skirts for confidence.

White clothes suggested a happier wearer than grey clothes did, with black clothes coming last.

These examples show how the impression changes with the question being asked: a blouse came out ahead for intelligence, while a onesie came out ahead for happiness.

The researchers began by asking about 200 people what they thought clothes could tell them about someone and comparing their answers with traits examined in previous research.

They then gathered ratings on 5,000 photographs from online shops, covering five kinds of impressions: intelligence, confidence, trustworthiness, happiness and sexual interest.

Participants formed these impressions from photographs of the garments alone, without seeing anyone wearing them.

The results indicated that who was doing the judging explained more of the variation in ratings than which garment they saw.

For example, one person might associate tracksuit bottoms with training for a race, while another might picture someone spending a Sunday on the sofa.

The researchers draw a parallel between judging people by their clothes and judging them by their faces:.

“That is, much like inferences from faces, the inferred attributes often lie in the eye of the beholder.”.

The study was published in the Journal of Computational Social Science (Rosenbusch et al., 2021).

Sources indicate that psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • I run a few faceless short-video channels (TikTok, Reels, Shorts), and they all had the same problem: they looked like everyone else's.
  • The result is an open-source repo with 18 identities, each proven by 2–3 real shorts rendered by code (45 in total), and a single prompt that turns any of them into your own studio.
  • 18 identités visuelles pour vos vidéos courtes, prouvées par 45 vraies vidéos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I run a few faceless short-video channels (TikTok, Reels, Shorts), and they all had the same problem: they looked like everyone else's. Same template, same captions, same stock motion. So I asked an AI agent to explore the opposite: how many genuinely different visual identities can you build for vertical shorts, entirely in code — and can you prove they're different?

The result is an open-source repo with 18 identities, each proven by 2–3 real shorts rendered by code (45 in total), and a single prompt that turns any of them into your own studio.

18 identités visuelles pour vos vidéos courtes, prouvées par 45 vraies vidéos. Un prompt suffit pour donner son style à votre chaîne. Open source.

Ask an agent for "a cool visual style for my channel" and you get one style, described in adjectives, with nothing to check it against. What I wanted was a menu with evidence: several identities side by side, each one documented in the same format and backed by real renders, so the choice is made by looking, not by vibes.

So every identity in the repo ships the same things:.

Recent findings suggest that all of it is indexed in one machine-readable file. This is what an agent actually reads:.

In a recent development, signatureToPreserve and confusableWith are the two fields that matter most. They tell an agent what it must not touch when it adapts a style, and which neighbour it would drift into if it did.

The repo is the exploration; you don't fork it to run a channel. A script scaffolds a separate project from one identity — your draft identity, scene templates for the content families you need, the render toolkit and an operating manual for the agent. The README boils it down to one prompt:.

Recent findings suggest that under the hood, the agent ends up running something like this. Here's a real run from today — a geography quiz channel for teens, built on the weather-map style, borrowing a template from the arcade style for a family the weather map never proved:.

Yes, the tooling talks French — the project started for French channels. Note the warning on the borrowed template: a blend keeps one identity's signature and only borrows structure from the other. Mixing two signatures is exactly how you end up generic again.

According to recent reports, here's the part that surprised me. To check that the 18 styles really are different, the repo has a measured test: a colour histogram in Lab space (Bhattacharyya distance) plus an edge histogram (χ²), 8 frames per short, and for each short, "is its nearest neighbour a short of the same identity?".

In a recent development, it scores 41/45. The four misses:.

Sources indicate that taken at face value, that indicates liquid-chrome isn't a coherent style at all. So I ran a second test the way a viewer would: a fresh agent with no context got 72 anonymised frames — 2 shorts × 2 frames for each of the 18 identities, random file names, the key kept out of its reach — and one instruction: make 18 groups of 4 by style, not by subject.

In a recent development, it made 18 pure groups out of 18, 72/72 frames. Its own notes put the finger on why the metric failed: the liquid-chrome group "joins two quite different scenes (test tubes vs Newton's cradle), linked by the shared glossy iridescent 3D rendering and black ground", and the dark identities (neon lab, cosmos, topo relief, pixel arcade) "are neighbours in palette but separated cleanly by type and rendering technique".

Industry observers note that that's the lesson. A colour-and-edges metric sees palettes. A style is mostly geometry and type: the chrome reflections, the pixel grid, the perspective of a 3D flyover. Two shorts of the same style on different subjects can have very different palettes (a blue ocean and a green mountain, for the pixel flyover), and two different styles can share a black background. I kept the metric — it's cheap and catches regressions — but the blind judge is now the evidence that counts.

It's a style menu and a production toolkit, not a channel in a box. Topic writing, fact-checking, review, publishing and scheduling are still yours (my own channels run those in a separate private template piloted from Notion; this repo only feeds it the style). And the agent can't hear: it measures loudness and checks timings, but someone still has to watch and listen to every episode.

Rendering is CPU-bound and uneven: from under 5 s per 100 frames (cut paper, single-line drawing) to around 3 minutes for the three.js space documentary, and over 5 minutes for one Manim chalkboard short — measured with several renders sharing a 4-core machine.

Everything is open source — the 18 design systems, the 45 shorts and their code, the render/voice/QA tools, and a Claude Code skill (fabrique-identites) that runs the whole "scout → adversarial challenge → studio → review" loop to add latest identities.

If you build a studio from it, I'd love to see which style you picked.

When Does Semaglutide Form Fibrils? What Circular Dichroism Can Tell You

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in one solution, semaglutide formed long, twisted fibers.
  • Sources indicate that semaglutide was back in the news on November 14, when Novo Nordisk declared its REDEFINE 9 results for CagriSema, its investigational combination of cagrilintide and semaglutide.
  • In a recent development, I’d start with Figure 2b.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in one solution, semaglutide formed long, twisted fibers. In another, the same peptide formed small, round clusters called micelles. What caught my attention in Valeria Castelletto and colleagues’ semaglutide study was that you could see a change in the acidic sample before you ever looked at a microscope image. If I saw that change in a formulation screen, which sample would I send for imaging, and when?

Sources indicate that semaglutide was back in the news on November 14, when Novo Nordisk declared its REDEFINE 9 results for CagriSema, its investigational combination of cagrilintide and semaglutide. The fibril finding comes from a separate March 31 paper. That team studied research-grade semaglutide in water. Its conclusions apply to those preparations, and the stability of the trial formulation and marketed products was outside the scope of the work.

In a recent development, I’d start with Figure 2b. The researchers used an Applied Photophysics Chirascan to measure far-ultraviolet circular dichroism (CD). The shape of a CD spectrum tells you about the way the peptide backbone folds, averaged across the molecules in the sample.

In a recent development, look at the fresh semaglutide trifluoroacetate solution at 1% by weight and pH 2.4. Its spectrum had two dips, one at 208 nm and another at 222 nm, characteristic of an alpha helix. After 40 days at 4 °C, the curve had one broad dip near 216 nm, consistent with a shift toward beta-sheet structure. That answers one part of the timing question. The peptide had changed by day 40. To find out how early that change was detectable, I’d want the samples from the weeks in between.

One detail I’d borrow from their experimental setup is the choice of quartz cells with light paths of 0.01 or 0.1 mm. A shorter light path lets more far-UV light through a concentrated solution. That matters here because semaglutide’s assembly depends on concentration. Diluting a sample to get a cleaner spectrum could change the very thing you’re trying to measure.

According to recent reports, take a look at Figure 1c and the close-up in Figure 1d. The cryogenic transmission electron microscopy images show long, narrow fibers in the acidic sample. In the close-up, you can see the twist. Small-angle X-ray scattering gave the team a second check on shape across the solution. A long-cylinder model fit the acidic sample, while the data for the base form of semaglutide at pH 8 supported micelles.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a reason I’d keep imaging in the blueprint even if two spectra look similar. In an earlier semaglutide study, the aged sample still had a helical CD signature, yet the researchers found a small population of short fibrils alongside the micelles. CD is good at showing when the overall structure has shifted. If a small population of fibers would change your formulation decision, it’s worth looking for those fibers directly.

According to recent reports, A study of the GLP-1-like peptide G48 took that next step. The researchers tested whether adding polysorbate 80 would help G48 keep its structure under conditions that caused it to aggregate. Their Chirascan Plus spectra revealed that G48 retained its helical shape with the additive at all three pH values tested.

Industry observers note that the result I’d want beside those spectra is the 72-hour comparison in Figure 7. Without a stabilizer, the team found no soluble monomer left at any of the three pH values. With polysorbate 80, they measured little to no loss of soluble monomer over the same period. That gives a formulation scientist two reasons to advance that condition for G48. The peptide kept its helical structure, and it stayed in solution as individual molecules.

In a recent development, suppose two formulations start with the same spectrum, but only one develops a broad dip near 216 nm during storage. I’d repeat that comparison with independently prepared samples, the same peptide concentration and a matching blank for each formulation. I’d also check for cloudiness because light scattered by particles can distort a CD spectrum.

Recent findings suggest that this is where I see a place for Chirascan in a formulation lab. Three formulations, four storage time points and two independent preparations already give you 24 samples, each with a buffer to account for. For a panel that size, Applied Photophysics reports that its automated Chirascan Q100 can measure 48 buffer–sample pairs in 24 hours. That makes it practical to keep the intermediate time points that a fresh-versus-aged comparison misses.

Recent findings suggest that I’d use Chirascan to choose a pair of samples for the microscope: the first time point with a reproducible change and the one immediately before it. I’d include the matched formulation that held its original spectrum. Seeing fibers at day 40 tells you where the sample ended up. Knowing whether they were already present when the CD curves first diverged tells you where to focus the next round of formulation work.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lower inflammation is associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.
  • Lower inflammation is associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.
  • People who score higher in conscientiousness or extraversion tend to have lower levels of certain markers of inflammation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lower inflammation is associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.

Lower inflammation is associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.

People who score higher in conscientiousness or extraversion tend to have lower levels of certain markers of inflammation.

Among the qualities that make up conscientiousness, being hardworking and organised stood out.

For extraversion, which includes both sociability and energy, the clearest result was for people who described themselves as active.

These patterns matter because inflammation that stays elevated over time is linked to both physical and psychological health.

Lower levels of long-term inflammation are linked to a lower risk of heart disease, stroke and premature death.

They have also been associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.

The researchers pooled data from six studies involving more than 19,000 adults in the United States, England and Japan.

Participants rated how well words such as ‘organised’, ‘hardworking’ and ‘active’ described them.

The researchers then looked at how those answers related to two markers of inflammation in blood samples, C-reactive protein and interleukin-6.

Earlier research had already linked higher conscientiousness with lower levels of both inflammatory markers (Luchetti et al., 2014).

In this study, people who described themselves as organised or hardworking tended to have lower levels of both markers.

Being hardworking showed the strongest association within conscientiousness, even stronger than the association for the overall trait score.

People who scored higher on extraversion tended to have lower C-reactive protein, and much of that association came from how active they said they were.

In fact, being active was more strongly associated with lower C-reactive protein than any other characteristic the researchers examined.

Being talkative showed a small association in the opposite direction, while being lively was associated with lower levels of both inflammatory markers.

In several of the studies, the association with being active held up even after the researchers took other aspects of extraversion into account.

Being active and hardworking may both reflect how much energy people have for everyday tasks.

In earlier research, people who scored higher on the activity aspect of extraversion or the achievement-striving aspect of conscientiousness tended to have better aerobic capacity during a brisk walking test (Terracciano et al., 2013).

Regular physical activity could help explain part of the association with inflammation.

The relationship could run in the other direction, too, if people with higher inflammation feel less energetic and come to see themselves as less active or lively.

The study was published in the journal Psychoneuroendocrinology (Stephan et al., 2026).

#80601. Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2339 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Linebender ↗ Open Full Page

Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2339 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Linebender

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs, published 4.5 years ago.
  • The motivation to build GUI apps in Rust remains strong.
  • Adoption of Rust UI in the past few years has been slow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs, published 4.5 years ago. The world is different in many ways, but some of the advice there is still valid. There have been roughly 20 Rust GUI toolkits announced since that blog post (see 2026 survey), but also a recent rapid acceleration of interest in Rust GUI, fueled by AI.

The motivation to build GUI apps in Rust remains strong. Many shipping GUI apps suffer from poor performance, especially when built with cross-platform technology. GUI toolkits shipped by platforms have largely stagnated, and system vendors remain uninterested in solving the cross-platform problem, so Electron has grown in popularity. RAM remains expensive and the focus is shifting to mobile, so bloat has real consequences. Building high-performance UI in Rust is a practical alternative.

Adoption of Rust UI in the past few years has been slow. Few flagship apps use Rust for their UI. One of the most notable is the Zed editor, built on their own GPUI framework. It proves that shipping Rust UI is practical, and indeed, GPUI is emerging as a major choice for AI-driven rewrites, most notably Discord. My personal sense is that GPUI is well suited to the Zed use case, and shipping in a real project boosts its visibility and credibility quite a bit, but it’s not necessarily the ideal choice for more general purpose applications. Among other things, its 2D rendering engine is well suited to a text editor, but lacks full gradient support, blending, filters, and other features expected of a renderer in the same class as Vello or Skia.

The reasons for slow adoption may be melting away. Writing Rust code is harder than languages more traditionally used for UI (TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift), and finding engineers skilled in both Rust and UI is challenging. But AI is changing the game. There’s evidence that the LLM cost of writing Rust code is not significantly higher than other languages, and there is reason to believe that in large codebases, Rust will be more maintainable because its type system helps enforce invariants. So if all languages have roughly the same cost, then why not go with one that has a dramatically better combination of safety and performance?

For these reasons, Rust is rapidly becoming the language for AI rewrites of existing codebases. But there is still no consensus on the strategy for the UI layer. I predict there will be a small explosion of trying lots of different things.

My 2022 blog post had a large section on “native,” first pointing out that the term has no clear meaning, and more broadly pointing out that “native” UI toolkits are simply choices among many, and should be evaluated on the vital quality criteria.

I think this is largely still true, but it depends greatly on which platform is being targeted. Windows still has no clear native choice (see Microsoft Hasn’t Had a Coherent GUI Strategy Since Petzold) and on Mac there is a bit of fragmentation between AppKit and SwiftUI. However, SwiftUI has performance issues (see Michael Tsai blog from 2025) and so it is clearly possible to do better on the performance front.

While desktop UI has remained stagnant, the situation on mobile is a bit different. Platforms continue to invest, and there are many fine details that are key for an app to look and feel native. One very notable example is Liquid Glass on iOS – if you use UIKit or SwiftUI, you can get that with little effort, but apps built with cross-platform toolkits won’t quite seem right. In addition, making gesture recognition, scroll dynamics, and IME 100% match the platform are not yet fully solved problems.

Thus, for mobile, an extremely viable path is to use the native toolkit for UI but do the common “business logic” in Rust. I’m not sure about the business logic, but for the UI, this is the decision that Shopify has made recently, abandoning React Native. I believe 1Password has this architecture. This is also the "Phoenix" plan for Discord on mobile, while using GPUI on desktop.

That mentioned, there's been considerable progress in trying to build mobile UI entirely in Rust. Below is a short screencast of the editor demo in android-view. You can see that a lot of IME functionality works, including swiping, moving the cursor by rolling the space bar, and deleting in semantic chunks. Not shown in the video below, but composition regions (needed for CJK) also work, and there's basic accessibility through AccessKit.

According to recent reports, one of the big unsolved problems as of the 2022 blog post was text layout. It is of course a hard problem to get right. I’m pleased to say that the ecosystem now has a good solution, in the form of Parley. It’s gotten there as a result of sustained investment from Google, Canva, and Dioxus (now Cognition), as well as contributions from the community. It seems to be used in the majority of new Rust UI toolkits. In addition, to help mitigate the risk of monoculture, Cosmic Text is a viable alternative.

AccessKit was just getting started in 2022, but is now solid infrastructure as well, and used by most UI toolkits. I should note, though, there is a difference between a good integration and a box ticking exercise. And there is more work to be done, for example to make rich text editing fully accessible. One other problem I'd like to see addressed is performance degradation when accessibility is enabled. This is a problem for egui in particular, as it has to build and diff a tree each animation frame, undercutting the benefits of its underlying immediate mode design.

One topic I talked about extensively in the 2022 blog post is leveraging the system compositor. This issue is even more pressing today, especially with the increased importance of video. You really want a video playing in a hardware accelerated layer when possible, and on low end devices it’s the only hope for getting smooth frame rates.

There has been some progress, notably the subduction library, but it certainly isn’t commonly integrated into UI toolkits yet. To do it well is a challenging problem, as the capabilities provided by the platform vary widely. Ideally there’s a rich and high level interface, something like CALayer on Apple platforms, and polyfills to implement that interface as well as possible on other platforms. On Android, when the task is something simple, like overlaying some GUI controls on a video, it would use SurfaceFlinger layers, but when it involves more sophisticated compositing, it would run shaders on the GPU.

This is absolutely something we should build, ideally as a high quality community project rather than something with dozens of vibe-coded forks. But even in the latter case it’s better for it to exist than not.

According to recent reports, one of the challenges of the Rust UI ecosystem is that different applications have different needs. The idea of a single, unified UI for completely general purpose use may be behind us, especially now that LLMs can optimize and fine tune for specific use cases.

That’s been playing out architecturally in the choice between immediate mode and retained mode. Immediate mode is very appealing because it’s less total code and seems quite a bit simpler. And for some applications (most especially development support for games) it works well. However, I am concerned it won’t scale especially well. In short, it’s good at the first 90%, but it makes the second 90% harder. To be considered really production-ready, it has to establish stable widget identities to build and patch the accessibility tree, and it has to reliably cache expensive intermediate artifacts such as text layouts (simple immediate mode often gets around this by cutting corners in text layout, which may be fine for gamedev). And of course, it pulls strongly towards a model of re-rendering everything every frame rather than exploiting layers in the compositor.

For this reason among others, I am not impressed by the choice of the ArtCraft projects to use egui. I do think egui is a really good implementation of the immediate mode paradigm in Rust, and it does solve a number of problems (including accessibility, something mainline Iced does not yet support), but it wouldn’t be my first choice for productivity and design applications. The egui README is quite honest on the advantages and disadvantages, and is worth consulting.

It has been revealed that one theme that’s emerging from trying to do LLM-assisted software engineering well is having clearly scoped modules, ideally with solid specifications of what the module does. Within a module, given clear objectives such as performance and robustness against adverse inputs, an LLM can do very well.

Industry observers note that this philosophy is in tension with what has historically worked well. People reasonably choose a UI toolkit based on how good it looks. In particular, Apple UI frameworks have an immense amount of design knowledge baked in, especially in the defaults. With very little effort, it’s possible for a developer to make an app that looks and feels like a Mac app, even if not very polished.

Recent findings suggest that I think in the future we should be moving toward a separation of design and execution. Both are hard problems, but very different. I’m especially excited about how much room there is to improve the execution side when really optimizing. As discussed in the 2022 blog post, the computer science core of a UI toolkit is an incremental computation engine.

Industry observers note that having a good spec at the interface between design and execution is critically crucial. As a general strategy, I suggest adapting web standards, but not following them slavishly. Web standards are an impressive and important artifact. A huge amount of time and energy has gone into producing them, and there’s also a lot of care to making things work cross-platform. The extensive WPT tests are the true magic of the spec, aiding correctness in the multiple high quality open source implementations. All this goes a long way to explaining why Electron is popular.

That stated, strictly adhering to web standards has serious downsides. DOM is slow and memory-intensive; a lighter weight tree representation with a bulk mutation interface might serve the need of GUI apps better. Full CSS style resolution and layout is also expensive, though CSS is a rich and powerful way to describe styling. A subset of CSS carefully curated for efficiency might be useful. I’ve done experiments in implementing selectors as an efficient state machine that supports incremental evaluation, at the expense of fancier CSS features such as sibling selectors.

The Web is also lacking a solid way to represent virtualized lists, a core feature of every efficient UI toolkit. A spec here requires nailing down the interface with the data model, preserving incrementality.

Blitz, as a modular browser engine, is well placed to serve as the cornerstone of hybrid approaches borrowing heavily from Web specs, but also adapting them to be higher performance and more tightly integrated with platform capabilities. As just one example, it’s possible to start with Stylo as the CSS selector engine, and then replace it with a leaner, more efficient CSS engine if that proves to be practical.

One good example of separation of concerns into smaller modules is the Xilem/Masonry split. The Xilem reactive layer was designed to be independent of the actual elements it controls, and indeed it has instantiations both for DOM (which, among other things, is the infrastructure for the squircle interactive demo) and Masonry widgets. Masonry, on the other hand, was designed to be independent of the reactive layer and indeed the language for the layer above it.

By contrast, SwiftUI mashes together the low level widget implementation, the reactivity framework, and the language as well; Swift runtime reflection is part of the execution engine. Obviously SwiftUI has had a lot farther reach than Xilem, but my argument today is that we should reconsider assumptions as things are rapidly changing.

Given a UI design encoded in a certain way – which can be code, data, or a combination of the two in a DSL – an engine has a number of opportunities to optimize the execution of that design. Perhaps a lot of this section is gilding the lily, as a straightforward evaluation of the design in optimized Rust code will outperform almost any shipping GUI. But I’m interested in the limits of what performance is possible. Can we get silky smooth UI even on low end Android phones? I think the answer is yes, and the question worth exploring.

It has been revealed that one useful tactic may be separating out the static from the dynamic parts of the design, and precomputing the static parts. That in no way precludes the design having dynamic parts; it's just that it may be possible to avoid the cost of a fully dynamic implementation.

Another fruitful avenue for optimization is optimizing the use of layers, to be composited either using the system compositor or a lightweight GPU-accelerated polyfill. Using layers effectively can dramatically improve performance, mostly by avoiding re-rendering of parts of the interface that haven't changed. However, layers have a RAM cost, and using too many layers can actually slow things down, as allocating newly introduced layers has to go through calls to the underlying system. Getting this right is a tricky optimization problem, and a good use of either measurement or analysis. UI toolkits generally either use heuristics, which are not always perfect, or explicit hints (like .drawingGroup() in SwiftUI or RepaintBoundary in Flutter).

For a deeper dive into performance questions, see A Critique of GPUI. Ideally, there aren't huge performance differences between UI toolkits, as all low hanging fruit should be picked. We expect implementations of system languages to be quite comparable in performance, but still tolerate wide discrepancies in GUI performance.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Energy, mood or sleep lost to worry? A UK survey found a clearer winter pattern for one of the three.

According to recent reports, energy, mood or sleep lost to worry? A UK survey found a clearer winter pattern for one of the three.

Low energy is the clearest sign of the winter blues among three symptoms studied in young people in the UK, ahead of low mood and losing sleep over worry.

Low mood is also more pronounced in winter, although the difference is smaller.

Shorter days may play a part by shifting the body clock and affecting when young people feel alert, while changes in exercise and social routines could also contribute.

The researchers analysed almost 6,000 interviews with over 4,000 people aged 16 to 24 who took part in the UK’s Understanding Society survey.

They compared interviews conducted in December, January and February with those conducted during the rest of the year, using data from 2022 and 2023 for the main analysis.

On a 0–100 scale, the average score for low energy was about 3 points higher in winter, while the score for low mood was about 2 points higher.

The estimate for sleep lost through worry was smaller and compatible with no seasonal difference.

The figures describe differences between survey reports collected at different times of year, so they give a picture of the group average rather than trace how any one person’s symptoms changed.

Earlier Canadian survey research found that a wider range of depressive symptoms varied by season among young people than among older adults (Lukmanji et al., 2020).

Sleep schedules continue to shift through adolescence and into early adulthood, so the timing of daylight may influence when young people feel most alert.

Winter can also change the shape of an ordinary week, with fewer chances to be active outdoors or spend time with friends in person.

Feeling short of energy could make it harder to stay engaged through a day of lessons or a long shift, even when the person’s mood has barely changed.

The study was published in the journal PLOS ONE (Guan et al., 2026).

Two Everyday Drink Swaps Are Linked To Less Weight Gain

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years.
  • Sources indicate that swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years.
  • Swapping sugary drinks for water is linked to less weight gain over time, according to a study of more than 140,000 adults.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years. What mattered was which drinks people gave up.

Sources indicate that swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years. What mattered was which drinks people gave up.

Swapping sugary drinks for water is linked to less weight gain over time, according to a study of more than 140,000 adults.

Replacing them with diet drinks highlights much the same pattern.

Switching from diet drinks to water was linked to a much smaller difference in weight.

Both swaps could make a difference by cutting the calories people get from their usual soft drinks.

A diet version can also preserve the familiar sweet taste, which may make the change easier for some people to stick with.

The findings suggest that the drink someone gives up may matter more for their weight than which of these two alternatives they choose.

The researchers drew on three long-running US studies that followed nurses and other health professionals for a typical period of 28 years.

Participants regularly reported what they drank and how much they weighed, allowing researchers to see how their drinking habits and weight shifted over four-year periods.

The researchers estimated about 1.4 kg less weight gain over four years when three sugary drinks a week were replaced with either water or diet drinks.

The estimated difference for replacing three diet drinks a week with water was only about a tenth of a kilogram over the same period.

People who cut back on sugary drinks tended to gain less weight whether or not they increased their intake of diet drinks.

The researchers estimated the swaps from changes in people’s reported habits, so the study can show associations but cannot establish how much weight any individual would gain or lose after making the switch.

Replacing a regular soft drink with its diet version changes the calories while keeping much of the experience of having a sweet drink.

Switching to water also removes the sweet taste, which may change how much sweetness people prefer over time.

In a separate year-long randomised trial, people assigned to replace sugary drinks with unsweetened ones showed a greater drop in their preferred level of sweetness than those assigned to artificially sweetened drinks (Ebbeling et al., 2020).

That change in taste preference offers a possible reason why an unsweetened choice might become more appealing with time.

The study was published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition (Espinosa et al., 2026).

The will vs trust decision is primarily a financial calculation: does the upfront cost of a trust save more than it costs by avoiding probate?

Industry observers note that when you die with only a will (no trust), your estate must go through probate — a court-supervised process where a judge validates your will, your executor inventories assets, debts are paid, and remaining assets are distributed. Probate costs include:.

Probate also takes 6-18 months on average and is a public proceeding — anyone can look up your will, your assets, and who inherited what.

A revocable living trust costs $1,500-$5,000 upfront but avoids probate entirely. The math is straightforward:.

Recent findings suggest that even with a trust, you still need a pour-over will — a short document that catches any assets not transferred into the trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. You also still need a healthcare directive and durable power of attorney. Most estate blueprint packages include all four documents together.

The FI-optimized approach to estate planning minimizes cost without sacrificing protection:.

Start with an online will now. A $159 Trust & Will plan gives you a will, healthcare directive, and power of attorney today. Do not let perfect be the enemy of done — having a basic will is infinitely better than having no will while you save up for an attorney.

In a recent development, upgrade to a trust when your net worth exceeds $200,000. At this point, the probate avoidance savings justify the $1,500-$3,500 cost of adding a trust.

Sources indicate that shop attorney fees aggressively. Estate planning is a competitive market. Get quotes from at least three attorneys. Many offer flat-fee packages, and prices can vary by 50-100% for the same work in the same city. Ask specifically whether the quote includes trust funding assistance and deed transfers.

It has been revealed that use online services for updates. Rather than paying an attorney $200-$500 for a codicil, many online platforms let you update your will for free or for a small annual subscription ($19-$39/year). Trust & Will, for example, includes one year of free updates.

It has been revealed that bundle documents. An estate plan package (will + trust + POA + healthcare directive) typically costs 20-40% less than purchasing each document separately. If you are going to see an attorney, get everything done in one engagement.

Here is the counterintuitive truth: the most expensive estate plan is the one you never create. Dying without a will (intestate) triggers state default rules that may not match your wishes, longer and more expensive probate proceedings, and potential family conflict. For parents of minor children, it means a judge — not you — decides who raises your kids. The $0-$259 cost of an online will is trivially small compared to these consequences.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

If your net worth exceeds $200,000, a $2,000-$3,500 revocable living trust saves your family $10,000-$35,000 or more in probate costs and 6-18 months of waiting. That is a 300-1,000% return on a one-time investment. For anyone on the path to financial independence, this is one of the highest-ROI financial moves you can make. The trust also provides privacy (wills are public, trusts are not), seamless incapacity planning, and immediate asset distribution to your beneficiaries without court involvement.

In a recent development, yes. FreeWill (freewill.com) offers a free basic will funded by nonprofit partners. Some states also accept handwritten (holographic) wills that cost nothing. Military personnel can get free wills through the JAG office on any military installation. Many bar associations and legal aid societies offer free will clinics several times per year. While these free options work for simple estates, you may want to pay $99-$259 for a more comprehensive online service that includes healthcare directives and power of attorney.

Sources indicate that attorneys charge $300-$750 for a simple will and $750-$1,500 for a complex will with special provisions. A complete estate initiative package (will, trust, power of attorney, healthcare directive) runs $1,500-$5,000. Fees vary significantly by location — attorneys in major metros charge 2-3 times more than attorneys in smaller cities for the same work. Always ask for a flat fee rather than hourly billing for estate planning.

For straightforward estates, yes. Major online will makers like Trust & Will, Nolo WillMaker, and LegalZoom produce documents that are legally valid in all 50 states and cover the same core elements an attorney would include. The difference is that an attorney can provide customized advice, handle complex situations, and anticipate concerns specific to your state law. If your estate is simple, an online will is functionally equivalent. If your situation has any complexity, the attorney consultation is worth the additional cost.

Online services typically include free updates for one year and then charge $19-$39 per year for ongoing access. An attorney charges $100-$500 for a codicil (formal amendment) or $300-$1,000 to draft a new will. For minor changes, a codicil is sufficient. For major changes (new spouse, additional children, significant asset changes), creating an entirely new will is cleaner and reduces the risk of conflicting instructions.

Industry observers note that if your estate is under $100,000-$200,000 with no real estate, a will alone is often sufficient. Once your net worth exceeds $200,000 or you own real property, a revocable living trust typically saves more in probate avoidance ($15,000-$70,000 on a $500,000-$1,000,000 estate) than it costs ($1,500-$5,000). A trust also provides privacy, avoids the 6-18 month probate timeline, and manages your assets if you become incapacitated. For most FI-focused households building significant wealth, a trust is the better long-term choice.

Recent findings suggest that the most expensive part of estate planning is NOT the documents — it is probate. Probate costs 3-7% of your estate value ($15,000-$70,000 on a $500,000-$1,000,000 estate) and takes 6-18 months. By comparison, even the most expensive estate blueprint package ($5,000-$10,000) is a fraction of what your family would spend navigating probate without a trust. The second most expensive mistake is outdated beneficiary designations on retirement accounts, which can send six or seven figures to the wrong person with no legal recourse.

Recent findings suggest that the cost of a will ranges from $0 to $10,000+ depending on your method and complexity, but the most expensive option is always having no will at all. For most FI-focused households, start with an online will for $0-$259 to get basic protection in place immediately. As your net worth grows beyond $200,000, invest $1,500-$5,000 in a comprehensive estate plan with a revocable living trust — the probate savings alone deliver a 300-1,000% return. Upgrade your beneficiary designations today (free), review your plan every 3-5 years, and remember: the goal of estate planning is not to create perfect documents. It is to protect the people you love from financial chaos during the worst moment of their lives.

  • In a recent development, when stress builds up and life feels overwhelming, we often forget to just breathe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

We all have those days. Your boss just dumped a ton of extra work on your desk, your kids’ school just told you they need to dress up as an ancient Greek philosopher tomorrow, a friend is texting about a personal crisis, and the fridge is empty, so you’ve got to fit in a grocery run. It’s… a lot.

In a recent development, when stress builds up and life feels overwhelming, we often forget to just breathe. But slowing down to focus on your breath can be a simple way to find calm and feel in control again.

Sources indicate that breathing exercises give you tools to manage stress, ease anxiety, and even boost your mood. These breathing techniques are quick to learn and can be done almost anywhere, whether you’re sitting in traffic, lying in bed, or taking a quick break at work.

In a recent development, in this guide, we’ll go through 10 types of breathing exercises, show you how to practice them, and explain how they can help. Here’s where to start.

Breathing exercises are simple techniques that help you take control of your breath. When we’re stressed or anxious, our breath usually speeds up, which can actually make us feel more anxious. But doing some focused breathing can help interrupt the cycle in a way that naturally calms your body and mind.

Industry observers note that there are lots of techniques, and they each work a little differently or have a particular area of intention. Some breathing exercises are best for reducing anxiety, while others can help improve focus, ease muscle tension, or even prepare you for a good night’s sleep.

Many people use breathing exercises to help in a challenging moment  or simply as part of a regular daily routine to help them keep stress at bay, sleep better, and make it easier to stay calm and focused throughout the day.

Sources indicate that you may be wondering if something so simple can really solve all your problems. And the answer is no —they can’t fill your shopping cart or complete that work project—but they can support your physical and mental health in more ways than one.

Reduces stress and anxiety: Breathing exercises calm the body’s stress response, quieting anxiety and helping you feel more centered.

Improves focus and concentration: Taking a few deep breaths can help sharpen your focus, so you can stay present and engaged.

Helps manage emotions: Focusing on your breath promotes a sense of calm and control, so you can handle emotions better. Struggling with your emotions? Check out these nine emotional regulation tips.

Boosts physical health: Certain breathing exercises can help improve lung capacity, circulation, and even immune response.

Supports better sleep: Breathing exercises like 4–7–8 breathing can help you fall asleep faster and improve the quality of your sleep (these six tips before bed can help too).

Boosts mood and mental wellbeing: Certain techniques, like resonant breathing (which is when you breathe slowly and evenly, usually around 5-6 breaths per minute), can improve your mood and overall sense of wellbeing.

Provides a sense of control: Breathing exercises remind you that even in challenging moments, you have the power to calm yourself.

It has been revealed that when life feels busy or overwhelming, having a variety of breathing exercises in your back pocket can be incredibly helpful. Since each exercise works a bit differently, being familiar with a few means you'll be better able to support yourself in any situation, whether you’re looking to calm down, get focused, or ease into sleep.

It has been revealed that as one of the simplest yet most effective ways to calm your body and mind, this technique is especially useful when you need to relieve stress, feel more grounded, or prepare for a restful night’s sleep. If you’re struggling to sleep well, try pairing breathing with these 10 tips to improve your sleep quality.

Industry observers note that how to practice: Find a comfortable position, either sitting or lying down. Place one hand on your belly to help you feel each breath as you inhale deeply through your nose, allowing your stomach to rise as you fill your lungs. Hold your breath for a couple of seconds, then slowly exhale through your mouth, feeling your belly fall. Repeat this pattern for about five to ten breaths, letting your body relax with each exhale.

💙 Learn an easy way to practice deep belly breathing with the Balloon Breath meditation, great for kids and adults!

This type of breathing can help strengthen your diaphragm and improve your body’s ability to take in oxygen. It can be particularly helpful if you're dealing with respiratory issues or you want to ease physical tension (these six tips can also help).

According to recent reports, how to practice: Place one hand on your chest and the other right below your ribs. Breathe in deeply through your nose, aiming to move only your diaphragm (your belly should rise while your chest stays relatively still). Exhale slowly through pursed lips, feeling your belly lower. Practice this for about 5–10 minutes.

A favorite among people who need to manage stress on the go, box breathing helps balance oxygen levels, slow your heart rate, and swiftly shift your body into a calm state, making it ideal for high-stress situations.

How to practice: Visualize a box where each breath segment represents one side. Inhale slowly through your nose for a count of four as you imagine progressing up the side of the square, hold your breath for another four along the top of the square, exhale for four as you move down the box, then pause for a final count of four to return to the start point. Continue for a few rounds, focusing on maintaining an even rhythm.

This technique is designed to calm the nervous system and ease anxiety. It’s particularly useful for winding down at the end of the day, so you're feeling ready for sleep. If you’re looking for more sleep support, check out these eight breathing exercises.

According to recent reports, how to practice: Breathe in through your nose for a count of four, and hold your breath for a count of seven. Breathe out slowly through your mouth for a count of eight, aiming for a gentle, complete exhale. Repeat this sequence three to four times, allowing yourself to fully relax.

Alternate nostril breathing can help balance energy, ease stress, and improve focus. It’s a great choice when you’re feeling mentally or physically drained and need a quick reset.

Sources indicate that how to practice: Sit in a comfortable position and place your left hand on your knee. With your right thumb, gently close your right nostril and inhale deeply through your left nostril. Close your left nostril with your ring finger, release your right nostril, and exhale fully through the right side. Inhale through the right nostril, close it, then exhale through the left. Continue this alternating pattern 5–10 times.

💙 Let Mel Mah guide you through an alternate nostril breathing practice during the Immune Strength for Optimal Health session.

In a recent development, this technique can increase oxygen flow to the lungs, which can be especially helpful if you have respiratory issues. It’s also calming, so it can ease anxiety and reduce shortness of breath.

In a recent development, how to practice: Breathe in through your nose for a count of two, then purse your lips as if you’re blowing out a candle and exhale slowly for a count of four. Keep the exhale gentle and controlled. Repeat several times, focusing on making the exhale twice as long as the inhale.

Industry observers note that the lion’s breath exercise releases tension, particularly in the face and jaw, while also boosting energy and clearing mental fog. It’s an energizing technique that’s great for moments when you feel sluggish or want to improve your mood rapidly.

How to practice: Take a deep breath in through your nose. Next, open your mouth wide, stick out your tongue, and forcefully exhale with a loud “ha” sound. Focus on releasing any tension from your face, jaw, and throat. Repeat 3–5 times, letting yourself feel fully present with the exercise.

Also known as coherent breathing, resonant breathing can help calm your nervous system and improve heart rate variability, which is an indicator of how your body adapts to stress and recovers. It’s a great technique for anyone looking to manage stress in the long run.

How to practice: Breathe in deeply for a count of five and then exhale for a count of five, maintaining a steady, slow rhythm. Aim to take about six breaths per minute, or whatever pace feels comfortable, and focus on keeping your breaths even and controlled.

Use this deeply relaxing technique to reduce frustration and tension. It can be particularly helpful for calming your mind before sleep or during moments of stress.

Industry observers note that how to practice: Sit comfortably, close your eyes, and take a deep breath in. As you exhale, make a gentle humming sound, like a bee, and focus on the vibrations in your head and face. Repeat this pattern five to ten times, letting the vibrations soothe your mind.

💙 Practice the humming bee breath in The Daily Move’s Wake Up Your Voice.

According to recent reports, breath counting is a mindful technique that brings you into the present moment, as counting the breaths can quiet racing thoughts and promote relaxation. This helps relieve stress and improve your focus.

How to practice: Mentally count “one” on the inhale, and then exhale normally. Then count “two” as you breathe to inhale, then silent on the exhale. Keep going all the way up to 10 and then start over again at one. Try this for about 5–10 minutes, focusing on the rhythm of your breathing. If you lose count, start at one again.

💙 Learn to Count the Breaths with guidance from Jeff Warren and The Daily Trip.

Practicing breathing exercises daily is the best way to see results. Even just a few minutes every day can help you feel calmer, more focused, and better able to manage whatever stress comes your way.

Many people find that practicing in the morning helps set a positive tone for the day, while an evening practice can be a great way to unwind and relax before bed, so try both to work out what fits best with your life. And if you’re looking to improve your daily routine, check out these tips to build your morning, workday, and evening routines..

If daily practice feels like too much at first, try starting with just 5–10 minutes a few times a week, as every bit counts toward building a sense of calm and balance.

Breathing exercises can be very helpful for managing anxiety and even calming a panic attack.

When anxiety hits, our breathing often becomes shallow and quick, which can make us feel even more anxious. Practicing slow, deep breathing helps break this cycle, sending a signal to your brain and body that things are okay. Try techniques like deep breathing, box breathing, and 4–7–8 breathing to calm your nervous system during anxious moments.

If you struggle with anxiety or panic attacks, learn breathing techniques in a relaxed setting first. Being familiar with the exercises makes it easier to use them when you’re feeling anxious, so you can start to feel in control and more grounded in tougher times.

Several breathing exercises can be particularly helpful for improving sleep.

Sources indicate that if you’re having trouble sleeping, set aside just a few minutes before bed to practice techniques like 4–7–8 breathing and humming bee breath, as they're known for their calming effects on the nervous system. These exercises can slow down your breathing and heart rate, making it easier to relax and drift off to sleep.

Surprisingly, certain breathing exercises can support your physical fitness and endurance. Techniques like diaphragmatic breathing, pursed lip breathing, and resonant breathing can improve lung capacity, which can help your body use oxygen more efficiently.

When your lungs are stronger and your breathing is steady, you can perform your favorite sports and exercises better, whether that’s walking, hitting the gym, football, dancing, or any other way you like to get active.

In fact, many pro athletes use breathing techniques to improve their performance and recovery time, so if you want to improve your endurance, try practicing regularly. You can do them either before a workout to warm up your lungs or afterward to help cool down and recover.

When you’re feeling stressed, techniques like box breathing, deep belly breathing, and 4–7–8 breathing can be especially helpful as they’re designed to promptly calm your body and mind.

Box breathing uses equal counts of inhale, hold, exhale, and pause, which creates a steady rhythm that helps quiet anxious thoughts.

Deep belly breathing slows your breath and encourages your muscles to relax.

The 4-7-8 technique calms the nervous system in order to calm the stress.

How Lead Exposure Erodes Long-Term Memory
